Vermont synagogue co-hosts fundraiser for Mohsen Mahdawi amid mounting scrutiny over extremist ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:50:24 UTC
01:50:24 KST

Beth Jacob, a synagogue in Montpelier, Vermont, joined forces with the Unitarian Universalist Church of Montpelier on Sunday to co-host a fundraising event supporting Mohsen Mahdawi, a Columbia University student and pro-Palestinian activist facing ongoing deportation proceedings.
According to the event listing published on the synagogue's website, the gathering at the Unitarian Universalist Church featured Mahdawi speaking on updates regarding his legal case, alongside guest speakers including constitutional lawyer and civil rights scholar David Cole, Harvard Divinity School Jewish studies professor Shaul Magid, NOFA Vermont executive director Grace Oedel, Vermont-NEA member benefits director Mark Hage, Middlebury College visiting professor Eric Levi Jacobson, and Unitarian Universalist Church minister Rev. Joan Javier-Duval.
Proceeds from the gathering were designated directly for Mahdawi's legal defense fund.
The event, however, drew criticism within the community. Investigative journalists Rachel Feldman, based in Vermont, and David Collier, based in the United Kingdom, previously published extensive findings in April 2025 and again in August 2026 detailing Mahdawi’s background, raising serious concerns regarding the decision of a Jewish institution to lend its platform and credibility to his defense.
Mahdawi’s legal battles began in April 2025, when US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents detained him at a US Citizenship and Immigration Services office in Colchester, Vermont, while he was attending a pre-scheduled appointment for his naturalization test.
Rather than facing criminal charges, Mahdawi was targeted under a rarely used provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. Section 1227(a)(4)(C)(i)), which allows the Secretary of State to initiate removal proceedings against a noncitizen whose presence or activities are determined to carry potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences.
Then-secretary of state Marco Rubio invoked this provision, citing Mahdawi's campus activism and pro-Palestinian protests at Columbia University following the October 7 attacks.
Legal, political challenges surround Mahdawi's detention
Mahdawi's detention sparked immediate legal and political challenges. While federal district judges initially intervened to secure his release from custody, the legal landscape shifted significantly in mid-2026. The Board of Immigration Appeals ruled that the government had provided sufficient evidentiary backing for his removal, and an immigration judge officially ordered his deportation to Jordan in June 2026.
Mahdawi subsequently appealed the decision to the US Court of Appeals, while federal appeals panels reinstated aspects of the government's authority regarding his custody status.
While Mahdawi's supporters have widely portrayed him as a progressive student leader targeted for exercising his freedom of speech, investigative work by David Collier and Rachel Feldman paints a portrait that contrasts sharply with that narrative
According to Collier and Feldman's findings, the autobiographical personal narrative Mahdawi has shared across various media outlets, including CBS 60 Minutes and other publications, contains significant factual inconsistencies when cross-referenced against historical records from the Second Intifada, such as B'Tselem casualty databases and weekly updates from the Palestinian Center for Human Rights.
Specifically, the investigators claim to have found that Mahdawi's accounts regarding childhood incidents, such as the reported death of a best friend and the circumstances surrounding family members killed during the conflict, did not match recorded historical events, noting instead that the relatives he mourned were active combatants killed while launching attacks against Israeli forces rather than innocent civilians.
Furthermore, the investigative reports uncovered extensive online activity from a public Facebook group created and managed by Mahdawi alongside his mother, Abeer Shamali.
The uncovered digital record documents content stretching from 2012 through 2014, coinciding with the period Mahdawi was preparing to relocate to the United States, wherein Mahdawi and his family systematically promoted a program titled In the House of a Fighter, glorifying and honoring individuals linked to Palestinian terrorist organizations, including members of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) and the al-Aqsa Martyrs Brigade.
Among the material highlighted in the investigation was a video posted to Mahdawi's group featuring his mother participating in the infamous "Khaybar" chant, a slogan allegedly threatening violence against Jewish people.
Some Beth Jacob members push back against synagogue co-hosting fundraiser
As documented in Collier and Feldman's investigation, the decision by the Beth Jacob Social Action Committee to co-host the fundraiser and invite Mahdawi for a pre-event discussion triggered immediate pushback among some of its own membership. When concerned congregants circulated the researchers' findings across the synagogue's internal mailing lists, leadership faced mounting pressure to address the red flags surrounding the event.
According to the published investigative records, rather than engaging with the documented evidence, prominent supporters within the synagogue sought to deflect criticism. Eric Jacobson, a synagogue member and scheduled speaker at the fundraiser, dismissed Collier's investigative credentials and questioned the researchers' linguistic proficiency in Arabic. In subsequent email exchanges documented in the reports, Jacobson questioned whether Collier was on the payroll of Israel's Ministry of National Security.
The investigative files further detailed that when concerns continued to mount regarding the hosting of an individual associated with the glorification of terrorism, synagogue leadership ultimately postponed an initial in-house reception. Writing on behalf of the Social Action Committee, organizer Alice Silverman acknowledged that members held significant concerns, but explicitly stated that an event to address those issues "would serve a very different purpose than what we are hoping and planning for on August 9, which is to show our full support."
Collier and Feldman claim in their report that attempts by independent researchers and concerned members to open a dialogue with synagogue organizers were met with institutional resistance. According to the journalists, leadership demonstrated no interest in discussing the documented evidence, choosing instead to push forward with an unconditional expression of solidarity for Mahdawi while attempting to silence internal dissent.
"There is more about Mr. Mahdawi that has yet to come to light," Feldman told The Jerusalem Post. "Despite the voluminous amount of local backlash I’ve received since we published, I’d rather keep the community informed and be hated for it than let them blindly cheer for someone whom I firmly believe has no good intentions for Vermonters or Americans.”
The Beth Jacob Board also spoke to the Post, saying, “The Beth Jacob Synagogue Board supported our Social Action Committee’s request to help organize a fundraiser for a Vermont resident, Mohsen Mahdawi, because we believe the US government has violated his rights of free speech and due process.”

Israel and Venezuela have agreed to renew consular relations following a series of talks between Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar and Venezuelan Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia in recent weeks and days, marking a significant step in restoring practical ties between the two countries.
Under the agreement, Israel and Venezuela will establish a coordination mechanism to facilitate the provision of consular services to citizens of both countries. The renewed consular framework is expected to enable the two governments to address practical issues affecting their citizens, including consular assistance and related services.

Following the earthquakes, an Israeli aid delegation traveled to Venezuela to assist with the emergency response and recovery efforts. The delegation was led by Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Israel Defense Forces’ Home Front Command, providing professional expertise in emergency management and reconstruction.
The renewed cooperation comes against the backdrop of a broader effort to establish practical channels of communication between Israel and Venezuela, even as the two countries remain without full diplomatic relations.
In their joint statement, Israel and Venezuela also mentioned the importance of the relationship between the State of Israel and Venezuela’s Jewish community.
The agreement represents a notable development in Israel-Venezuela relations and opens a new channel for continued contact and cooperation after more than 15 years without diplomatic relations.

The groups assert that the financial and legal penalties against the ICC have forced them to “curtail a wide range of human rights and legal work in violation of their First and Fifth Amendment rights under the US Constitution and under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act”.
Other organisations joining the lawsuit are the American Friends Service Committee, the Centre for Constitutional Rights and the Open Society Institute. The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

He said that if the situation continues to unravel, it will undermine the implementation of Resolution 2803 (2025) and erode the prospects for realising a negotiated Israeli-Palestinian peace based on the two-state solution, urging the immediate implementation “in full” of Resolution 2803, together with the New York Declaration.

The gospel according to Bibi: How Israel Christ-washes hasbara
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:48:00 UTC
01:48:00 KST

Breadcrumb
The gospel according to Bibi: How Israel Christ-washes hasbara
For years, Israel sought to distinguish itself from the “Middle Eastern muck”, as political scientist Ian Lustick puts it. Instead, it sought to present itself as the region’s only democracy and, later, as an entrepreneurial, high-tech society. Its public diplomacy now appears to be cultivating another, yet rather questionable, distinction: being the protector of Christianity in the Middle East.
The effort has gained momentum against the backdrop of Israel’s deteriorating international image following the Gaza genocide and the attacks on Lebanon. But it has been building for months, if not years.
In late 2025, Israel allocated up to $4.1 million for a campaign targeting evangelical Christians in the United States, while in December its foreign ministry helped bring more than 1,000 evangelical pastors and Christian influencers to Israel.
For over a decade, Netanyahu has touted Israel as a place where Christians “thrive”, contrasting it with their “persecution elsewhere in the Middle East”, most recently in an April Easter message. Weeks later, the Israeli Foreign Ministry appointed George Deek as its special envoy to the Christian world.
What about Palestinian Christians?
Yet many of the people at the centre of this “diplomatic campaign” tell a very different story. The Israeli state presenting itself as Christianity’s protector has presided over the erosion of one of the region’s oldest communities, Palestinian Christians.
The Christian presence in Palestine predates the arrival of Islam by centuries, and many of today’s Palestinian Muslims are rooted in the same indigenous population that gradually converted to Islam. This continuity is visible in towns like Bethlehem and Beit Jala, where Muslims and Christians have lived and thrived alongside each other for centuries.
This long Christian presence makes their marginalisation a relatively recent phenomenon, closely intertwined with the political transformations of the modern era. European powers repeatedly invoked the pretext of protecting Christian communities to justify imperial intervention in the Middle East. But the decisive rupture, and the onset of their demographic decline, came with Zionism.
After decades of transformation driven by Zionism and facilitated by the British Mandate authorities, the Nakba of 1948 displaced roughly 750,000 Palestinians, setting Palestinian Christianity on a trajectory of decline from which it has never recovered.
Christians in Palestine numbered roughly 89,000 in 1931, about 9% of the population, rising to 145,000 by 1946. The Nakba shattered this thriving community, and around 90,000 Christians were displaced, churches closed, and homes and property lost, alongside their Muslim compatriots.
The 1967 occupation deepened the process. When Israel occupied the West Bank and Gaza, Palestinian Christians in the two territories numbered more than 42,000, around 6% of the population. By 1997, they were roughly 40,000 (1.5%); their share fell to 1.2% in 2007 and roughly 1% by 2017, even if their numbers increased slightly.
The contradiction is perhaps most stark around the places Christianity holds sacred. In 2002, Israeli tanks surrounded Bethlehem’s Church of the Nativity for 39 days, and did not hesitate to fire at the compound and set part of it ablaze. It was an unsettling tableau, Christ’s peaceful sanctuary encircled by Merkavas, engulfed in smoke.
The impact of genocide
During the Gaza genocide, the Israeli knife was sharper and pressed harder against everyone’s neck. Christian or Muslim, church or mosque, there was nowhere to hide from the slaughter and blind bombs. Gaza’s Saint Porphyrius Church, one of the world’s oldest continuously active Christian churches, was struck by Israeli warplanes, killing 19 people sheltering there. The pattern continued in July 2025, when the Israeli army fatally bombed Gaza’s Holy Family Catholic Church.
Meanwhile, in Jerusalem, the contradiction is visible at street level. Spitting at Christian clergy and pilgrims has become a recurring form of harassment, particularly among some Jewish extremists. That alongside verbal abuse and vandalism.
Taken together, the decline cannot be explained simply by birth rates or religious tensions. Palestinian Christians live under the same occupation as their Muslim compatriots, facing restrictions on movement, land confiscation, settlement expansion and political insecurity. These conditions have also constrained economic opportunity, making emigration increasingly attractive to a community with established networks abroad.
And this history is precisely what Israel’s Christian diplomacy seeks to obscure. Its effort to present itself as the protector of Christians serves two interchangeable purposes: separating Palestinian Christians from the Palestinian national story and, second, recasting the conflict in religious terms.
The first requires erasing a history that contradicts the state’s narrative. Ignoring that Palestinian Christians were deeply involved in the national movement long before the Nakba.
The role of Palestinian Christians in the liberation struggle
Khalil al-Sakakini, an Arab Orthodox intellectual from Jerusalem, became one of Palestine’s prominent nationalist voices, while Issa and Youssef al-Issa founded Falastin in Jaffa in 1911, an influential Arabic newspaper that opposed Zionism. Even the term “Nakba” was popularised by the Christian Palestinian intellectual Constantin Zureiq.
This role continued into the 1960s and 1970s, when Palestinian Christians were prominent in the secular, Arab-nationalist and Marxist currents of the resistance, and within the PLO. George Habash, a Palestinian Christian, for instance, founded the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP).
That tradition continues today. Palestinian Greek Orthodox Archbishop, Atallah Hanna, remains an fierce critic of the occupation, and had his share of Israeli abuse. Much like Palestinian Christian journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, whose killing by Israeli forces in Jenin in 2022 was followed by the violent desecration of her funeral in Jerusalem.
Meanwhile, the second purpose of ejecting Palestinian Christianity from local history is to portray the Palestinian struggle for freedom as essentially Islamist. Within this framework, Palestinians become less a national population resisting dispossession and more Muslims confronting Jews.
The framing is straightforward. Once a conflict is coded primarily in religious terms, people tend to interpret its participants through those categories. This places Israel within the Western narrative of the struggle against Islamic extremism. Netanyahu has repeatedly cast Israel as part of a broader Western struggle against “militant” or “radical Islam”, portraying Israel and the West as confronting a common civilisational threat.
Contradictions
The Islamisation also gives anti-Semitism a broader political reach, allowing Israel to invoke Western sensitivity to antisemitism as a form of political leverage.
A Palestinian Christian disrupts that mental shortcut: he is Palestinian, but not Muslim; Arab, but Christian; and capable of sharing the same national grievances as his Muslim neighbour.
But once the intellectual debate is put aside, what remains most contradictory in Israel’s narrative is the lives of many Palestinian Christians themselves. And most of us Palestinians have a story or two to tell about that.
I still think of our next-door neighbour in Gaza, Fadi, who was killed by an Israeli bullet while taking part in a demonstration against the occupation during the First Intifada. I did not even know he was Christian until his funeral.
None of that mattered. What joined us was not only that we were Palestinians, but the shared experience of affliction and dispossession. The grievances shared by Fadi’s family were no different from ours; their stories of displacement were ours. His grandparents and ours had walked the same Via Dolorosa after being driven from their towns and villages during the Nakba, hunted down by Jewish militias.
Fadi was carried to his final resting place on the shoulders of the same youngsters who had carried the local mosque attendant, killed by Israel a few weeks earlier.
We used to say, Fadi baptised the land with his blood.
That is perhaps the simplest answer to Israel’s claim on Christians.
Dr Emad Moussa is a Palestinian-British researcher and writer specialising in the political psychology of intergroup and conflict dynamics, focusing on MENA with a special interest in Israel/Palestine. He has a background in human rights and journalism, and is currently a frequent contributor to multiple academic and media outlets, in addition to being a consultant for a US-based think tank.

Iran's supreme leader just overhauled its military leadership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:47:19 UTC

Breadcrumb
Iran's supreme leader just overhauled its military leadership
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has appointed six senior commanders to key positions across the country's military establishment, reshaping the leadership of the armed forces and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) after several top commanders were killed in the US-Israel war on the country.
The appointments, announced on Monday, fill some of the most powerful positions in Iran's security apparatus following the deaths of senior military leaders in US-Israeli strikes that began on 28 February.
They also offer an early indication of the figures Khamenei is turning to as Iran rebuilds its military command after the war.
The reshuffle came a day after Khamenei appointed IRGC veteran Mohsen Rezaei as head of the Supreme National Security Council. Rezaei served as commander-in-chief of the IRGC from 1981 to 1997.
So who are the six commanders taking on some of Iran's most important military positions?
Ahmed Vahidi, commander of the IRGC
Brig Gen Ahmad Vahidi has been promoted to major general and formally appointed commander-in-chief of the IRGC.
Vahidi has been a prominent figure within the organisation for more than four decades and previously commanded its overseas operations arm, the Quds Force, for about a decade before Qassem Soleimani took over in 1998.
He later moved into government, serving in several senior positions, including as defence minister and interior minister.
Vahidi is regarded as a central figure within the IRGC's hardline establishment and had acted as its de facto leader since Maj Gen Mohammad Pakpour was killed on the opening day of the war.
Israel and Western governments have accused Vahidi of involvement in overseas attacks, including the 1994 bombing of a Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires.
Ali Abdollahi, army chief of staff
Maj Gen Ali Abdollahi has been appointed to lead Iran's regular armed forces, known as the Artesh.
Abdollahi has served in both the regular military and the IRGC and most recently commanded the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, a body central to coordinating Iran's military operations.
He replaces Lt Gen Abdul Rahim Mousavi, who was killed during the initial US-Israeli attacks on 28 February.
Hossein Taeb, head of the Basij
Cleric Hossein Taeb has been appointed head of the Basij, the IRGC's volunteer paramilitary force, which has played a central role in suppressing domestic dissent and enforcing the Islamic Republic's social restrictions.
Taeb is one of the most powerful figures to have emerged from the IRGC's intelligence and surveillance apparatus.
He headed the organisation's intelligence arm for 13 years before leaving the position in 2022.
Mostafa Izadi, deputy commander of the IRGC
Maj Gen Mostafa Izadi has been named deputy commander-in-chief of the IRGC, serving directly under Vahidi.
Izadi is a veteran commander who has held positions across both the IRGC and the Artesh since the late 1980s.
His appointment makes him the second-highest-ranking commander in the Revolutionary Guards under its newly installed leadership.
Kioumars Heydari, army deputy chief of staff
Brig Gen Kioumars Heydari has been appointed Abdollahi's deputy in the Artesh.
Heydari most recently served as deputy commander of the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters. Before that, he commanded the army's ground forces for nine years.
Israel reportedly attempted to assassinate Heydari during the Twelve-Day War in 2025.
Ali Azmaei, IRGC navy commander
Adm Ali Azmaei has been appointed commander of the IRGC navy, putting him in charge of the force at the centre of Iran's military operations in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.
A veteran of the Iran-Iraq war, Azmaei has spent the past two decades in senior naval positions and served as deputy commander of the IRGC navy before his promotion.
He replaces Alireza Tangsiri, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike in March.
The IRGC navy has assumed particular importance during the current confrontation because of Iran's efforts to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important shipping routes.

The ministry gave a slightly smaller toll, saying four had been killed.
The transport ministry in its statement said it "held the Houthi terrorist militias fully responsible for the deaths, injuries and damage inflicted on the commercial vessel 'Tihamah' as well as for the serious consequences resulting from these attacks."
There was no official comment from the Houthis about the alleged attack.
The incident comes after a years-long truce in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government collapsed last month as fighting flared between Iran and the United States.
The breakdown of the U.N.-backed 2022 accord came as the Houthis announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, hitting Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and the kingdom's oil infrastructure, in parallel with Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Netanyahu’s video did not mention the major earthquake that struck Colombia over the previous day.

Policy is at the heart of the energy challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:43:22 UTC
01:43:22 KST

With the development of artificial intelligence (AI) products and the expansion of semiconductor manufacturing, Taiwan needs more electricity — along with a stable, low-carbon and resilient energy system. The challenge is meeting the growing demand without reducing energy discussions to a simplistic debate over nuclear power.
While Taiwan faces power-supply pressures, the situation should not be mistaken for an energy shortage. Ministry of Economic Affairs data show that the operating reserve margin exceeded 10 percent on 342 days last year, and demand for electricity is forecast to grow at an average annual rate of about 2.5 percent until 2035. The real test is whether the government can increase capacity while maintaining a reliable, effective grid.
AI requires large amounts of electricity, but jumping from “AI needs electricity” to “AI needs nuclear power” lacks a sound policy basis. Data centers need more than just generating capacity — they also require reliable power, sufficient transmission and distribution capacity, a stable grid and predictable costs. The electricity issue is not simply whether power can be generated, but whether it can be delivered.
Nuclear power is a low-carbon electricity option, but whether it can immediately solve the power supply issue is a separate matter. A possible restart at the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant would not result in an immediate increase in available electricity, as the Pingtung County plant must first undergo safety reviews and other legal procedures.
Similarly, renewable energy might not be able to provide consistent, reliable electricity, but that does not justify dismissing it entirely. Different power sources, energy storage, energy-use management and smart grids should all be integrated into the power system.
Advocates can take stances, but energy policy cannot apply double standards. Nuclear power raises safety issues, and entails waste and decommissioning costs; harnessing renewable energy requires addressing land use issues, ecological impacts and grid integration problems, and natural gas must contend with import dependence, price volatility and carbon emissions. Every energy option must be subject to an assessment of costs, risks and responsibilities.
Taiwan needs an energy system with institutional resilience. How much energy is needed, when and where it is needed, how it would be delivered and who would bear the costs and risks are critical questions. More importantly, who would be held responsible if forecasts are inaccurate?
Mature energy governance is not about predicting what would happen 10 years from now — it is about ensuring that the system can adapt, substitute, recover and bear the burden even if forecasts are wrong.
While AI creates more electricity demand, the real test for Taiwan is not how many power plants can be constructed over the next 10 years, but whether it can cope with surging demand, extreme weather, fluctuations in energy prices and grid failures. This is the pragmatic and unavoidable energy challenge the nation faces.

====================================================================================================

The myth of  Anthony Bourdain: how the bad boy chef became a hero to boozehounds and bullies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:43:20 UTC
01:43:20 KST

The trope of the Angry Young Man was not born in a kitchen, but Anthony Bourdain’s particular myth-making created what might be the prototype for fin de (20th) siecle masculinity. As the director of Tony, the new biopic of Bourdain focusing on his first job, has said, the film is about “a magical world where nothing can go wrong and a young man who’s angry about it.”
Bourdain arrived in that job, as a dishwasher in a restaurant in Provincetown, Massachusetts, aged 19. He was hellbent on a life of formless, self-sabotaging rebellion, and found his tribe. But when he published his book Kitchen Confidential in 2000, a quarter of a century later, he set the ethos of that kitchen tribe in stone, and attracted an ever-replenishing pool of chefs who, if they weren’t already just like him, were prepared to die trying.
However, that anger, like everything about Bourdain, wasn’t real — it was performative, playful. He compared himself once to the chef Eric Ripert, saying they both had a “live and let live energy,” but Ripert “believes in karma … I believe in vendetta.” That fabled anger never sounded quite real.
Photo: AP
MISFIT SUBCULTURE
Kitchen Confidential starts with Bourdain traveling through France as a child with his brother and his moneyed American parents of European inclinations and heritage. He is a little prick to his family, for no reason, and he’s also a git to the French kids, before returning to the US to be a jerk to flatmates and girlfriends in his private liberal arts university (Vassar) before dropping out. He’s still in his teens in 1975, when he takes that lowly job in Provincetown. There, he’s a minnow among absolute sharks of delinquency — a chef might turn out an impromptu service for a 100-strong post-wedding party, then bang the bride against the bins afterwards. The staff scored drugs you’ve never heard of, and drugs you’d never have needed if you hadn’t taken all those other drugs.
In that kitchen, Bourdain finds his spiritual home, “a subculture whose centuries-old militaristic hierarchy and ethos of ‘rum, buggery and the lash’ make for a mix of unwavering order and nerve-shattering chaos,” he wrote in Kitchen Confidential. That book, remembers the journalist, cookery writer and cook Diana Henry, 63, described “a world we didn’t have an in on, and suddenly we did.” (Henry did, in my view, the best late-era interview with Bourdain, two years before his death.)
Photo: EPA
Bourdain described his cheffly mission: “Your body is not a temple, it’s an amusement park. Enjoy the ride.”
In his writing, as in his cooking, he prioritized pace and crunch over elegance and fuss. Relationships in this brigade system were tightly bonded and savagely caustic.
“As an art form, cook talk is, like haiku or kabuki, defined by established rules,” he wrote. “All comments must, out of historical necessity, concern involuntary rectal penetration, penis size, physical flaws or annoying mannerisms or defects.”
Between the drugs, the shagging, the late nights, the contradictory, hurtling imperatives of discipline and self-indulgence, the contempt for self-care and the penis jokes, this was a definitionally masculine ideal, and not even for so childish a reason as that you’d need a dick in order to dip it in someone’s Vichyssoise. There’s just no female model for being beautiful, high and still smashing it at work: the women in this space (just off the top of my head, Nancy Spungen, Amy Winehouse) end up dead.
In many ways, Bourdain was just saying what he saw: this was the reality of kitchens across decades and continents. Tom Kerridge, 53, describes being drawn in by exactly the same atmosphere.
“Every chef will tell you the same thing — they don’t come into kitchens because they love food. Chefs love the energy of being chefs. It becomes your way of life, as opposed to what you do — it’s what you are.”
Photo: Reuters
LIFE WITHOUT CONSEQUENCE
Kitchens might have their hierarchies imported from the French army, their insubordination penalties only a fraction less violent, yet at the same time, Kerridge continues, “they’re building sites, they’re construction zones, they’re full of people using sharp things and burning themselves, who are all really tired.”
Andrew Clarke, 48-year-old co-owner and exec chef at Acme Fire Cult in east London, and the founder of Glandstonbury (yes, it’s an offal festival), said of his first colleagues — nowhere fancy, a pizza place in Bluewater, in the late 90s: “They were these pirates. None of them were proper chefs. They needed a job without a CV, without any qualifications — some of them had been in prison, and the kitchen was very accepting of that.”
The word “pirate” is used constantly, by everyone, and the ex-con thing is real: in 2009 the Clink charity was established, opening restaurants in High Down, Brixton and a couple of other prisons, teaching prisoners skills for when they got out. And there’s a reason they were trained up for professional kitchens, not ice-cream parlors.
Clarke remembers arriving “in a kitchen that was very French, very disciplined, very trained. Bourdain’s book was just out, and I just started reading little passages, and I thought, ‘That’s me. That’s the person I am, that’s where I’ve been, that’s what I’ve done.’”
Sally Abe — 38, former head chef at the Pem in the Conrad, St James’s, London, and, lately, her own bistro, Teal — had an all-female senior team at the Pem, but did not enter the business in 2007 wanting to throw over its hyper-masculine conventions.
“To be honest, I’m a very stubborn, determined person,” she says. “When I was 21, I thought, ‘I can be one of the boys,’ and I got swept up in it. It was really fun.”
Yet at the same time, Bourdain’s writing was so vivid, his character so magnetic, his joie de vivre so complicatedly credible and so contagious, that he built the world in the act of describing it.
As much as it pains me to pour cold water over it, Bourdain’s myth — the bit that was neither rooted in reality, nor prefigurable by force of will — was that the quintessential chef’s life could just proceed without consequence.
“Bourdain romanticized that sort of life,” Henry says, “taking coke, drinking too much.”
He ended up in rehab in the early 90s, but remained a heavy smoker and drinker. In kitchens the world over, says Clarke: “All roads led to the bar: a good service, you go to the bar, a bad service, you go to the bar. I saw chefs being drunk in service, and quite often that was me. I’d have a skinful at lunch and then do a dinner.”
Kerridge has talked in the past about his jaw-dropping alcohol consumption, before he went teetotal in 2013.
In 2015, Clarke suffered a terrible depressive episode. When he posted about it on Instagram, a huge number of people in the industry shared their own experiences with him. He has since set up a mental health charity for people working in the hospitality industry called Pilot Light.
“While we wanted to raise awareness of mental health in the business, it inevitably led to people talking about bullying, sexism and racism in the industry. I’m a chef — I wanted to keep it very clean and simple. For me it was about mental health. But it was Pandora’s box.”
TOXIC MASCULINITY
It’s worth making a distinction between the ludic, juvenile macho vibe Bourdain immortalized and a more modern toxic masculinity, designed to undermine, control and exclude women (having come of age in the 90s, I could spend forever insisting on that distinction). However, Bourdain himself, a subtle and self-critical person, could see how the first provided cover for the second. As he told an audience at his alma mater, the Culinary Institute of America, in 2017: “If there’s a harasser in the kitchen who’s a jerk, chances are he’s got a copy of my book on his station. And I’m going to have to live with that.”
There were also a lot of real bullies operating under the cover of play-bullying, and it’s interesting, looking back, how widely this was accepted in the industry. It was an open secret when Noma — the experimental Danish restaurant — was huge in the 2000s that its founder, Rene Redzepi, terrorized his staff. When the New York Times published evidence in March that Redzepi had “punched employees in the face, jabbed them with kitchen implements and slammed them against walls” leading to “lasting trauma from layers of psychological abuse, including intimidation, body shaming and public ridicule,” the collective sound of people feigning horror at a thing that we’d all known for 20 years was really something.
That’s not just kitchens, of course.
“Not only does it look like an awful way to treat people, it’s become unacceptable,” Henry says. “You can’t bully anybody anywhere.”
She recalls her experience working as a TV producer on food programs.
“Even the way I behaved in television, making researchers stay late because they hadn’t done enough, I wouldn’t get away with that now. We don’t like it any more.”
Abe has no problem differentiating between mischief, intensity, ego and harassment.
“Kitchens are always going to be high-pressure places — once you’re in the service, you’re in the service. If the food’s not ready, you’re an idiot... My kitchen’s nothing like that now.”
Clarke is done with the macho bullying (“It’s deeply uncool,” he says), and when he started Acme in 2022, he did a thing that would doubtless have had Bourdain, back in the day, exploding in 2,000 colorful words.
“We have very physical, long days; none of us look after ourselves like athletes and perhaps we should. We were doing yoga classes in the space, checking in, talking to each other. Doing everything a little more holistically.”
It’s not as anti-Bourdain as it sounds, Clarke says: “He got into jiu-jitsu in his 50s. He was fully at the point of: ‘I’m going to look after myself.’”
Bourdain never understood his own propensity for self-sabotage, as well as other-people-sabotage. It’s laced through his writing: there he always is, making trouble for no good reason. And he said as much to Henry when she interviewed him.
“What is it that gave him the pain that he carried around with him?” she asks. “His childhood sounded perfectly OK. He was just always a bit of a wreck until he got to be a chef. It’s strict — you can’t not deliver. You’ve got to be in, you’ve got to see your crew, you’ve got to do your service. There are completely set rules and you can’t disobey them.”
Kitchens were a haven for people who needed rules as much as they hated them, and could only reconcile those warring urges in a cacophony of appetites.
Perhaps inevitably, through some combination of a little foresight and a changing world, the pirate spirit that defined kitchens for so long is being replaced by a new intellectualism.
“Chefs nowadays are like bloody poets,” Henry says. “Stevie Parle, Merlin Labron-Johnson — all these people have got degrees. Once they would have been doing a master’s and a PhD; instead they’re focusing on growth and animals and flavor combinations and technical stuff.”
It’s not a sanitized world. It surely still has the plenty of what Bourdain wrote were the fundamentals of “good food and good eating ... blood and organs and cruelty and decay.” An intellectual kitchen just doesn’t invite chaos, or torment, or madcappery, but you wonder what will become of all the people who were mainly in it for those things.

Every functioning country on Earth maintains a national archive to preserve its official records. In Taiwan, that institution is the National Archives Administration (檔案管理局, NAA), a unit of the government’s National Development Council. Since September last year, part of the NAA’s purpose-built headquarters in New Taipei City’s Linkou District (林口) has been open to the public. The National Archives (國家檔案館) store and showcase documents generated through the day-to-day operations of government agencies. Covering defense, education, economic development, health, and other policy sectors, what’s displayed here will appeal to anyone with an interest in the country’s history — although having some Chinese
Aug.10 to Aug.16 Yuko remembers getting into frequent fights with children from neighboring villages who called him huana (番仔), a derogatory term for Indigenous people meaning “savage.” “I was mad because they made fun of me. I had no idea that it had anything to do with my identity,” the Pataran (北投洋) resident in Tainan’s Jiali District (佳里) told me when I visited in 2019. Yuko’s experience was not unusual among the Siraya and other Pingpu (plains Indigenous) groups, who hid their Indigenous identity amid stigma and discrimination, leaving later generations unaware of their ancestry. When anthropologist Melissa J. Brown
In August of 1939 Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union concluded an agreement on credit that enabled trade between the two dictatorships to boom. This was followed by two economic agreements in February of 1940 and January of 1941. By the summer of 1940 the Soviet Union “had become the most important supplier of raw materials” to Germany, accounting for almost a third of its oil imports. A year later Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union, its most important trade partner. The great silence: why haven’t we found any aliens yet?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:43:20 UTC
01:43:20 KST

During a visit to the Los Alamos National Laboratory in 1950, Enrico Fermi, one of the architects of the Manhattan Project, was having lunch with other physicists when the conversation turned to flying saucers. At one point during the discussion, Fermi blurted out: “Where is everybody?” — or, as another participant remembered it, “Don’t you ever wonder where everybody is?” If aliens exist, in other words, why have we never encountered them?
The episode has become famous, marking the moment when extraterrestrial life went from a theme for philosophical speculation to a serious scientific problem. For centuries, people had wondered whether life exists on the moon or Mars, but they accepted that we would never know for certain, since making contact with another planet was impossible. By the 1950s, those limits no longer seemed so fixed. In addition to space flight, researchers were developing tools to detect the radio signals that reach us from stars many light years away. These developments were still in their infancy, but it was already clear that humanity was no longer bound to Earth the way it always had been.
This expansion of human horizons raised an awkward question. Since the 16th century, when Copernicus showed that Earth is not the center of the cosmos, modern science had learned to embrace the idea that there is nothing unique about our planet. And if Earth is statistically average, there is no reason why it should be the only home of intelligent life. Given the age of the universe — about 13.8 billion years, according to current estimates — it should be full of species with technology far more advanced than what we have come up with in a few thousand years of civilization. Yet we can’t find any trace of them.
Photo: Reuters
That was the case in 1950, and it is still the case today, despite well-publicized claims to the contrary. Since 2017, when the New York Times reported that the US military possessed video recordings of pilots’ encounters with UFOs, aliens have gone mainstream. The House of Representatives even held hearings on what are now called unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) as a potential national security threat. But the blurry and inconclusive “Pentagon UFO videos” have not been followed by any clear images of nonhuman craft, just as earlier waves of UFO sightings never produced any unambiguous evidence.
For most scientists, the real mystery about aliens isn’t their presence but their stubborn absence.
The first serious effort to detect radio signals from alien civilizations in deep space was made in 1960, when the American astronomer Frank Drake conducted an experiment he named Project Ozma. Using a telescope at the National Radio Astronomy Observatory in West Virginia, Drake looked for signals at a precise location on the electromagnetic spectrum: 1420 MHz, known as the “hydrogen line” because hydrogen atoms emit photons at that frequency.
Because hydrogen is so abundant in the universe, the line is easy for radio telescopes to detect. In a 1959 paper, astronomers Giuseppe Cocconi and Philip Morrison argued that this fact would be discovered at an “early stage in the development of radio astronomy” by any technological civilization, as it was by human beings. That made it likely, they reasoned, that any species looking to broadcast radio signals to attract the attention of cosmic neighbors would choose to do so at 1420 MHz. But though Project Ozma spent 150 hours observing two relatively nearby stars similar in size to our sun, it detected no unusual activity at the hydrogen line.
In 1971, NASA convened a panel of experts to study the best ways to search for extraterrestrial life. Their report, Project Cyclops, was published the next year, and has remained a kind of bible for the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (usually shortened to Seti) ever since. The report called for the construction of the Cyclops system, “an ‘orchard’ of antennas 10km to 10 miles in diameter and containing 1,000 to perhaps 2,500 antennas.”
Such an array could scan the sky 200,000 times faster than Ozma.
The cost of building Cyclops was estimated at $10 billion to $25 billion, the equivalent of $77 billion to $192 billion today, making it about as expensive as the Apollo program. It was never built, and Congress ended NASA’s modest funding for Seti projects in 1993. Since then all US efforts have been privately funded, mainly by billionaires such as Paul Allen, cofounder of Microsoft, and Yuri Milner, a Soviet-born entrepreneur. Advances in computer technology mean that today’s Seti efforts are vastly more sophisticated than half a century ago, able to examine millions of radio channels from tens of thousands of galaxies. But the result remains the same: no artificial signal from an alien civilization has ever been detected.
That doesn’t discourage true believers. Seth Shostak, an astronomer at the California-based Seti Institute, writes that Seti’s “failure is tempered by the fact that the number of star systems sampled is still quite small”. In 2010, astronomer Jill Tarter, one of the leading figures in the field for decades, calculated that so little of the universe had been searched that it was like dipping a single glass into the ocean to determine whether it contains fish.
If extraterrestrial signals are out there and it’s just a matter of looking in the right place, it’s entirely possible that Seti could find one tomorrow. But it hasn’t happened in more than 65 years of searching and, until it does, alien signals remain as hypothetical as alien spaceships. Not only is there no evidence that extraterrestrials are trying to contact or visit us; there is no evidence that they exist at all. And this non-appearance presents a more serious challenge to modern scientific assumptions than any UFO sighting. It turns out that there really is something unique about Earth: as far as we currently know, it is the only place where life exists. But why?
DRAKE EQUATION
In October 1961, a year after Frank Drake failed to detect any alien radio signals with Project Ozma, he invited a dozen scientists to a conference to discuss the future of Seti. To clarify the problem, he tried to calculate how many extraterrestrial civilizations could be broadcasting radio signals in our galaxy. The answer, Drake reasoned, depended on seven variables, including “How many planets in an average system are capable of supporting life?” and “On planets where life exists, how often does an intelligent species like humanity evolve?”
Multiply all of the variables and you get the number of potential targets for Seti in the Milky Way. Drake wrote out the formula, which has been known ever since as the Drake equation. At the time, none of the variables could be estimated with any confidence. Drake’s back-of-the-envelope calculations yielded an estimate of 50,000 transmitting civilizations, but this was essentially just a guess. The real purpose of the Drake equation was to establish a research program, a set of questions for astronomers to try to answer. In the 21st century, they have made significant progress, thanks to new space-based telescopes that make it possible to see the cosmos in more detail than ever before.
For the first variable — how fast are new stars formed in the Milky Way — it’s now estimated that 10 to 20 new stars are born every year (a far slower rate than when the galaxy was young and richer in star-forming gas). The total number of stars in our galaxy is on the order of 100 billion. In the visible universe as a whole, there are an estimated 2 trillion galaxies, yielding a total of about 100 sextillion stars. So much is still unknown about the universe that this figure is certain to be revised, but it’s sufficiently mind-boggling to get the Drake equation off to a promising start.
It is much easier to detect stars than the planets that orbit them, and in 1961 the answers to Drake’s second and third questions — how many stars have planets, and how many of those planets are potentially habitable — were completely unknown. As telescopes gained in power, it became possible to detect exoplanets — planets outside our solar system — by measuring the tiny variations in a star’s light caused by a planetary mass passing in front of it. The first exoplanet was detected in 1992, the second in 1995. The pace of discovery exploded in the 2010s, thanks to observations from the Kepler space telescope and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite.
As of last year, some 6,000 exoplanets have been identified in the Milky Way, including at least three orbiting Proxima Centauri, the closest star to the sun. This is just the tip of the iceberg. While it’s not yet possible to conclusively answer Drake’s second question, a study published in Nature in 2012 suggested a minimum of 100 billion planets in our galaxy alone.
ASTROBIOLOGY
To answer Drake’s third question — how many of those planets are capable of sustaining life — a new scientific discipline has emerged: astrobiology, the study of life among the stars. This is a paradoxical endeavor, since there are no examples to study. Instead, astrobiologists think about the basic conditions that make life possible, and how we might determine whether distant planets meet those conditions.
Exoplanets are far too distant to see what is happening on the surface. But it’s possible to measure the size of the planet and its distance from the star it orbits, and make deductions about its atmosphere and temperature — and, more indirectly, about its magnetic field. Since Earth is the only planet where we know life exists, it’s natural to assume that exoplanets that resemble it in these respects are the most likely to be habitable.
Astrobiological research thus also involves investigating life on our own planet, to understand the range of environments in which it can develop. The discovery of “extremophiles,” primitive organisms that thrive in extreme conditions, has shown that living things can flourish under two miles of ice and in hot springs that reach 98 Celsius. This suggests that life of some kind could develop even on inhospitable planets. For instance, while there is no liquid water on Mars today, frozen remnants of ancient oceans are thought to exist under its surface; it’s possible that some kind of extremophilic life could be detected by future probes.
NASA announced last year that a rock sample analyzed by the Perseverance rover included two minerals, vivianite and greigite, that on Earth are byproducts of bacterial metabolism. The minerals may be a sign that primitive microorganisms existed on Mars several billion years ago. If confirmed, this would be a revolutionary discovery. As the astrobiologist David Catling has written, “Even the simplest microbes native to Mars … would change the balance of probabilities that life exists elsewhere in the galaxy, for they would demonstrate that life can originate twice within one solar system.”
In fact, proof of life on Mars would not necessarily mean that it originated independently on two planets. It’s also possible that life could have emerged on Earth and traveled to Mars or vice versa, carried through space in meteorites or dust. That would be evidence for the “panspermia” theory, which holds that life originated in just one or a few places in the cosmos and then spread naturally over eons.
On Earth, any life form more advanced than bacteria requires liquid water to survive. Thus the most important criterion for a habitable exoplanet is that it can’t be too close to the star it orbits, where intense heat would evaporate water, or too far from the star, where cold would turn it into ice. If an Earthlike planet is inside the “Goldilocks zone” where the temperature is “just right” for liquid water to exist, it can be considered a candidate for life.
The first such planet to be discovered was Kepler-452b, seen by the Kepler space telescope in 2015. It is a bit larger than Earth and takes 385 days to complete an orbit of its star, very similar to our year of 365 days. By 2025, the Habitable Worlds Catalog, a database maintained by the University of Puerto Rico, included 29 Earthlike exoplanets, and the process of discovery has only just begun. A study published in the Astronomical Journalin 2020 estimated that the total number of Goldilocks-zone planets in the Milky Way is at least 300 million, and possibly as high as 6 billion.
Astronomy has made enormous progress in filling in the first three variables in the Drake equation. The difficulty, as the astronomer Sara Seager has written, is that “the first three factors … are measurable; the other four are not, and arguably never will be”.
The closest we can come to answering Drake’s fourth question — how many planets actually develop life — is to look for biosignatures, chemical compounds in the atmosphere of an exoplanet that on Earth are associated with the presence of life. Researchers announced last year they had found dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18b, an exoplanet in the habitable zone of a star 124 light years from Earth. Because that compound is produced on Earth by ocean plankton, it could be a sign of the presence of organic life. But the finding was quickly challenged by other scientists, who argued the data did not prove the presence of dimethyl sulfide.
K2-18b is a good example of the limits of astrobiology. To find an exoplanet is very difficult; to find one in the Goldilocks zone is even harder; to detect potential biosignatures is harder still. And even if biosignatures were to be definitively confirmed, it would only show that life may exist. There is no way to know whether it actually does, much less what form it takes.
The search for exoplanets is radically expanding our understanding of the cosmos.
“We have learned that the universe is teeming with a fascinating variety of planets, more types than we could have imagined,” writes the astrobiologist Lisa Kaltenegger.
But so far, it has found exactly as many extraterrestrials as radio astronomy has: zero. The more we learn about the universe, the more acute the Fermi paradox becomes.
EXPLAINING THE ‘GREAT SILENCE’
To explain this “great silence,” researchers focus on the last three variables in the Drake equation: on planets where life exists, how often does an intelligent species like humanity evolve? Of intelligent species, how many develop the technological ability to send radio signals into space? And finally, how long does a transmitting civilization last before it disappears?
These questions go beyond the limits of astronomy; they can’t be answered, even in principle, by developing more sensitive telescopes. The only way to shed light on them would be to assemble a catalogue of species across the cosmos and study their history. But the reason we have to ask Drake’s questions in the first place is that we don’t have such a catalogue.
In practice, then, thinking about extraterrestrial intelligence means thinking about the only intelligent species we do know — ourselves. What conditions had to exist for Homo sapiens to evolve and develop spacefaring technology, and how long can we expect technological civilization in its current form to survive?
Of the seven variables in the equation, Drake and his colleagues found that last one, which they called “L” (for “length of time”), the hardest to calculate, offering a range of estimates from 1,000 to 100 million years. This uncertainty reflects the fact that L is essentially a prediction about the future of humanity. As long as ours is the only technological civilization we know about, we have no way to estimate the longevity of such civilizations except to think about how long ours can be expected to last. And there is a good reason to think this may not be a long time. The birth of radio astronomy and space flight coincided with the invention of nuclear weapons; the same rocket technology that sent astronauts to the moon was used to build intercontinental ballistic missiles. Human beings have managed to avoid destroying ourselves in a nuclear war for the past 80 years, but it would be a bold prophet who would guarantee that we will not do so in the next 80, not to speak of the next 800. It is possible that technological progress is self-limiting: any species powerful enough to escape its planet is powerful enough to destroy it.
Drake thought that multiplying all the variables in his equation would yield about 50,000 transmitting civilizations in our galaxy. If the true number turns out to be just one, it follows that at least one of those variables must have a much lower value than expected. In other words, there must be one or more steps in the evolution of advanced civilization that are very difficult to surmount.
THE ‘GREAT FILTER’
As the economist Robin Hanson wrote in an influential 1998 paper, “There is a ‘great filter’ along the path between simple dead stuff and explosive life.” For some reason, “the vast vast majority of stuff that starts along this path never makes it. In fact, so far nothing among the billion trillion stars in our whole past universe has made it all the way along this path.”
Like the Drake equation, the great filter offers a structure for thinking about what makes technological civilization possible. Any answer to that question involves astronomy, physics and biology. It also leads to questions about human nature and destiny that have traditionally been the province of philosophy and religion.
That certain physical conditions are necessary for the development of life has been recognized for a long time: distance from the sun, the presence of water, a breathable atmosphere. But there are a multitude of other cosmic coincidences that may be equally necessary for life to develop and survive. For instance, any planet that is regularly bombarded by asteroids would find it difficult to sustain life for long. When a single asteroid about six miles in diameter struck the Yucatan peninsula 66 million years ago, it is thought to have extinguished three-quarters of all existing species, including the non-avian dinosaurs.
Such impacts would be much more common if not for the presence of Jupiter, a giant planet just the right distance from Earth to intercept comets and asteroids. A Jupiter-like neighbor may be a prerequisite for advanced life, since on a planet without one, the clock of evolution would be continually reset by mass extinctions.
Then there is the role of plate tectonics. The Earth’s surface is broken into large plates that drift very slowly over time. At their fault lines, old rock made of carbon is drawn into the planet’s hot interior and new rock is produced in the form of magma. This “conveyor belt” has the effect of stabilizing the level of carbon in the atmosphere, preventing runaway heating or cooling that could extinguish life.
Geologists aren’t certain why Earth has tectonic plates — the current best theory is that the decay of radioactive elements in the interior of the planet produces heat that melts subsurface rock. But we know that ours is the only planet in the solar system to have them. Mars and Venus, which are rocky and about the same size as Earth, have rigid surfaces that don’t break into separate masses. So it’s possible that plate tectonics, too, belongs on the list of prerequisites for life.
The more conditions life needs, the easier it is to whittle down the galaxy’s 100 billion planets as potential homes for it. The “rare-Earth hypothesis,” writes the Serbian astrophysicist Milan Cirkovic, holds that “each of these requirements [for life] is unlikely and they are (or at least seem to be) causally independent, so that their combination is bound to be incredibly rare and probably unique in the Milky Way.”
Life on Earth seems to have emerged fairly quickly after the planet was formed; the oldest bacteria are only a few hundred million years younger than the solar system. This seems like an encouraging sign that, under the right conditions, it is easy for life to get started. But after those early beginnings, major evolutionary milestones came very slowly. It took about 2 billion years for the first cellular nucleus to develop, enabling the transition from primitive prokaryotic bacteria to more advanced eukaryotes. Another billion years passed before the emergence of the first multicellular organisms.
Strikingly, genetic evidence shows that each of these crucial developments occurred only once in the history of life on Earth. This suggests that they may not be inevitable stages that life would pass through anywhere, but surpassingly rare accidents. Life may exist on other planets in the form of archaea — unicellular organisms that can thrive in extreme conditions — without ever evolving as far as sponges, much less plants and animals.
THE HARD PROBLEM OF LIFE
As for mammals like ourselves, our reign on Earth is also highly contingent. Dinosaurs were our planet’s dominant species for more than 150 million years. By comparison, Homo sapiens have existed for only about 300,000 years, 0.006 percent of the history of Earth. When we look back on the history of humanity from this point of view, we seem to see ourselves perched on a toppling Jenga tower of incredible coincidences. So many factors had to line up perfectly for us to come into existence; change just one and we would not be here. The effect is vertiginous, reminding us that everything we take for granted about our world is in fact radically contingent. Not only do life and human life not need to exist; it would be immensely more reasonable for them not to exist.
In centuries past, some thinkers came to a similar conclusion and saw it as proof of providence, which shaped the finely tuned structure of the cosmos to foster the evolution of humanity. Today, rather than turning to old supernatural doctrines to explain human uniqueness, a new generation of cosmologists argues that we need to radically expand our idea of the forms life and intelligence might take, and how we should go about looking for them.
Seti operates on the premise that we will find aliens because they want to be found. It looks for radio signals sent deliberately into space with the goal of attracting attention from civilizations advanced enough to detect them. The Project Cyclops report argues that “the sending race will attempt to make the job of deciphering and understanding the messages as simple and foolproof as possible.”
This assumption reflects the optimism of the space age, when humanity landed on the moon and gazed into deep space for the first time. Having accomplished so much so fast, it was natural to believe that other intelligent species would be equally venturesome. Wouldn’t they want to end their cosmic loneliness as much as we do?
Such ideas about how aliens would act are fundamentally anthropocentric, imagining that any intelligent species would be driven by the same motives we are: love of knowledge and love of power. But there is no reason why intelligent life elsewhere in the universe should have evolved to resemble us, either physically or mentally.
In a 2016 paper titled The “Hard Problem” of Life, physicists Sara Imari Walker and Paul Davies observe that “both astrobiology and our assumptions about non-human consciousness tend to be biased by our understanding of terrestrial life.”
We take for granted that the particular forms that evolved on Earth — “from the level of cells, to multicellular organisms, to eusocial and linguistic societies” — are the inevitable product of natural laws, so that something like them must emerge anywhere life exists. But Walker and Davies argue that, in fact, life as we know it is the product of “a combination of chance and necessity,” including many unlikely events that pushed the evolution of life on to new pathways.
Rather than expect all living things to look like us, with arms and legs and rocket ships and radio telescopes, Walker and Davies propose that we think about life in a new way, defining it in functional terms as “the actual physical mechanism that permits information to gain causal purchase over matter.” On Earth, information is encoded physically in DNA strands and synaptic impulses; elsewhere in the cosmos, it might take such different forms that we wouldn’t recognize it even if we found it.
This idea fascinated the 20th-century Polish science-fiction writer Stanis?aw Lem, who dramatized it in a number of novels and stories. In his best-known book, Solaris, humanity discovers a planet covered by a sentient ocean. The second chapter, The Solarists, is an elaborate imaginary history of scientific debates about this organism, which resembles a “syrupy jelly.” Is it a “primitive being” or a “highly organized structure”? Had it bypassed “all the terrestrial stages of development — that is to say, the emergence of protozoa and metazoa, plant and animal evolution” — yet still managed to become intelligent?
The novel develops into a kind of horror-thriller, as astronauts marooned on Solaris are stalked by bizarre apparitions. But these aren’t ghosts; they are attempts by the ocean-being to communicate with the visitors by reading their minds and adopting the shapes it finds there. The ocean itself seems to think by creating elaborate shapes and structures with its gelatinous waves. But the human visitors are totally unable to grasp the meaning of these movements. The real tragedy of Solaris isn’t the gruesome deaths of the scientists, but what one of them calls “the failure to make contact, the lack of response.”
ESCAPING PHYSICAL EXISTENCE
More recently, theorists and storytellers — a distinction that often blurs when it comes to thinking about aliens — have begun to speculate that what separates us from extraterrestrials isn’t different biologies. Rather, biology itself may be a primitive phase in the development of mind, which truly advanced civilizations inevitably outgrow. After all, the most impressive technological achievements of the 21st century have not been in space exploration, but in computing, which allows us to create ever more detailed and powerful models of the world. If this progress continues, we have begun to worry, artificial intelligence and virtual reality could replace human intelligence and material reality.
Perhaps this is why we have so far failed to find traces of alien life. When intelligent species are sufficiently advanced, maybe their goal isn’t colonizing planets, but escaping physical existence altogether. John Smart, a non-academic futurist who describes his work as “acceleration studies,” calls this the “transcension hypothesis:” aliens are invisible to us because they have transcended bodily existence as we currently understand it.
Presenting this idea in a 2012 paper, Smart speculated that as civilizations develop “more computation and simulation abilities,” they will expand not into outer space but into “inner space,” creating virtual realities more complex and interesting than physical reality. On Earth, computers have become ever more compact as they grow more powerful; so it makes sense to assume that the material substrate of alien virtual realities — the hardware on which the software of consciousness runs — will come to occupy less and less physical space. Ultimately, Smith argues, this process could yield a technology so compact that it will essentially disappear from the map of the cosmos.
It’s clear that the transcension hypothesis, like the cold war-era idea of galactic colonization, is a kind of presentism, assuming that whatever is happening now will continue to happen in the future, only more so. It elevates the computer revolution of the 21st century to a universal process that every technological civilization will follow.
But in thinking about extraterrestrial life, it’s hard to see how some degree of anthropocentrism and presentism can be avoided. In the absence of actual data about aliens, thinking about them is an act of imagination, and the only material our imaginations have to work with is our own experience. As our understanding of our species changes, so does our sense of what is probable or possible for our cosmic “others”. Just as accounts of UFO encounters are human testimonies, not scientific evidence, so all our thinking about aliens and how to find them is best understood as humanity’s evolving self-portrait.

Hungarian lawmakers were yesterday expected to elect former Supreme Court chief Andras Baka, who was fired under former prime minister Viktor Orban, as the nation’s next head of state.
The post became vacant following the contested removal last month of the previous president, an Orban ally, as pro-EU conservative Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar pushes to loosen his predecessor’s lingering hold over state institutions.
Magyar’s ruling Tisza party on Saturday nominated Baka — who served 17 years as a judge on the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) — for the largely ceremonial role.
Photo: AFP
Magyar said Baka’s life served “as an example of commitment to the democratic rule of law and constitutional principles,” as the central European country needs to be “guided back onto the path of the rule of law and constitutional governance.”
Tisza has the two-thirds parliamentary majority required to elect Baka, 73, on the first round without any opposition support.
The vote in parliament was due to star at 2pm.
The previous president, Tamas Sulyok, saw his mandate cut short by a constitutional amendment, adopted as part of Magyar’s reform push.
Magyar’s party won the elections in April, ending nationalist Orban’s 16 years in power and promising “system change.”
However, rights watchdogs criticized Sulyok’s removal, comparing the tinkering to the methods Orban used to build his self-styled “illiberal” system.
Orban’s Fidesz party, along with its ally KDNP, said they would boycott the parliamentary vote, saying Sulyok’s ouster was “tyrannical” and “illegitimate.”
Baka has not been critical of Sulyok’s removal, although he was terminated with a similar legislative act.
“In a country governed by the rule of law, such extraordinary measures cannot be used, but Hungary became a captured state under Orban,” he said last month.
State officials like the president “were appointed not to restrain the government’s power, but to ensure the political survival of the former system even after an electoral defeat,” Baka added.
Installing Baka as president signals a “guarantee that the restoration of liberal democracy will proceed along a clearly defined path,” said Bulcsu Zsiga, from the Center for Fair Political Analysis.
Besides a brief stint as a lawmaker, elected from the conservative Hungarian Democratic Forum’s party list in 1990, after the democratic transition, Baka did not hold any political positions.
He was a judge at the Strasbourg-based European Court of Human Rights from 1991 to 2008.
In 2009, he was nominated as the head of the Supreme Court, but was ousted in 2012 after he condemned a move under Orban to reduce the age of mandatory retirement for judges from 70 to 62, calling it a judicial purge.
The EU and the US called the age-limit reduction illegal, and in 2016 the ECHR ruled that Baka’s dismissal amounted to a violation of his freedom of expression.
“His nomination also carries a symbolic meaning, given that Baka went all the way to prove that what happened to him was not really in line with European Union norms,” Zsiga said.
Last month, Magyar offered the nomination as president to chess legend Judit Polgar, but she declined after the prime minister faced mounting outrage for not consulting the public as promised.
Magyar has indicated the new president would only serve part of his term, until the completion of a process to replace the Orban-era Basic Law with a constitution drafted through wide public participation.
Magyar has estimated rewriting the constitution would take one or one-and-a-half years, promising to launch consultations on it next month.

Prosecutors accused Xu and Chung of accepting instructions to campaign for certain political candidates, while Xu helped Sun and her friend Luo Ying (羅穎) enter Taiwan in October last year under the guise of a business exchange.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
The court in a news release said that Xu kept in contact with former Taipei deputy mayor Vivian Huang (黃珊珊) of the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) at Sun’s instruction.
Furthermore, after initiating contact with then-TPP chairman Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) in January 2023 ahead of his run for president, Xu learned of the party’s intention to establish a new immigrants’ committee, its desire to recruit her as its chair and its interest in including her on its legislator-at-large list, the court said.
Prosecutors also alleged that Xu handled NT$28.75 million (US$890,700) in unreported remittances, earning more than NT$240,000 in illegal proceeds.

During the trial, Xu admitted to fraudulent loan applications and illegal currency exchange activities, but denied breaching the Anti-Infiltration Act and covering up Sun’s visit to Taiwan.
Xu was released on NT$2 million bail and placed under electronic monitoring after the trial concluded on June 9.
She did not appear in court yesterday to hear the verdict.

Seventy-two severe cases of COVID-19 and 14 deaths related to the disease were confirmed last week, the highest weekly numbers this year, as hospital visits for COVID-19 also increased by 27.6 percent from the previous week, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday.
The centers also reported that influenza activity is gradually increasing, and might enter an epidemic period later this month
Respiratory pathogen monitoring data show that SARS-CoV-2 and flu viruses were the most common viruses circulating in the past four weeks, CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Deputy Director Lee Chia-lin (李佳琳) said.
Photo: CNA
The number of hospital visits for COVID-19 increased by 27.6 percent to 24,645 last week, she said, adding that cases continue to increase domestically, while global positivity rates are also rising.
People aged 65 or older accounted for 73.6 percent of severe COVID-19 cases reported last week, while people who have not been vaccinated since October last year accounted for 91.7 percent, Lee said.
The growth rate of COVID-19 cases last week slowed slightly from the 74.8 percent increase in the previous week, indicating that the current wave of infections is nearing its peak, CDC Deputy Director-General and spokesman Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said.
The CDC revised its previous forecast for weekly COVID-19 outpatient and emergency-room visits at the peak from 51,000 to about 27,000, with the peak expected later this month, he said.
Although the revised prediction has been scaled down, severe cases and deaths continue to increase, with the highest numbers reported last week, Lin said.
A man in his 60s who had cancer and received his last vaccine dose in 2023 was among the COVID-19 deaths last week, CDC physician Lin Yung-ching (林詠青) said.
The man tested positive for COVID-19 after experiencing chills earlier this month, and after his symptoms progressed rapidly, he was admitted to a hospital with difficulty breathing, chest discomfort, fever, coughing and lethargy, Lin Yung-ching said.
The man was diagnosed with pneumonia and low blood pressure, and died the following day, he said.
A one-month-old girl with severe COVID-19 was the youngest severe case reported since October last year, and remained in intensive care, he said.
She had congenital heart and lung disease and was not yet eligible for vaccination, he added.
People aged 65 or older, and people with chronic illnesses or suppressed immunity should get vaccinated for better protection against severe illness, and family members of infants younger than six months should also get vaccinated to protect infants, and should seek emergency treatment for an infant if the child shows signs of severe illness, he said.
Meanwhile, hospitals reported 92,075 visits for flu-like illness last week, while flu-like illness accounted for 10.5 percent of emergency-room visits, Lee said, adding that 70 severe flu cases and 12 flu-related deaths were also confirmed.
Visits for flu-like illness have been increasing for four consecutive weeks, and flu-like illness accounted for 10.5 percent of emergency-room — nearly the 11 percent epidemic threshold, Lin Min-cheng said.
The centers estimate that flu activity will enter an epidemic period in about one or two weeks, while the peak period is predicted for early or mid-next month, he said.
The CDC urged people to practice good hand hygiene and respiratory etiquette to protect themselves and others from respiratory diseases. People should avoid unnecessary outings when experiencing a fever or respiratory symptoms such as coughing, a runny nose or a sore throat, and should avoid crowded or poorly ventilated areas, or wear a mask.
