====================================================================================================

The Ceuta crisis is about more than migration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:43:14 UTC
01:43:14 KST

The sight of 72,000 people rushing into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from neighboring Morocco was a blunt reminder that one of the EU’s most sensitive land borders is in north Africa.
The status of Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish enclave within Morocco, has been a simmering political dispute between the Moroccan and Spanish governments for many decades. Morocco claims sovereignty over the cities, whereas Spain maintains that they are as much a part of its national territory as Madrid.
For centuries, the Muslim dynasties that ruled the western Maghreb and al-Andalus controlled Ceuta, until King John I of Portugal captured it in 1415 — a precursor to European expansion overseas. When the Portuguese monarchy came under the control of the Spanish Habsburgs in 1580, so, too, did Ceuta.
Following the restoration of Portuguese independence in 1640, the city remained loyal to the Spanish monarchy.
As the great French historian Fernand Braudel observed, the Mediterranean should be understood as a historically interconnected theater, shaped by migratory, commercial, cultural and political exchanges that long predate the modern nation-state. From that perspective, the Strait of Gibraltar is not merely a border, but a liminal zone between two shores of the same sea that have long been in close, if often conflictual, contact.
To support its sovereignty claim, Morocco points to precolonial history and the continuity of the Moroccan Sultan’s authority over extensive territories in the western Maghreb. Moroccan historians, notably Abdallah Laroui, have also emphasized the need to avoid mechanically applying the territorial categories of the contemporary nation-state to precolonial societies.
The modern European conception of the border as a precisely demarcated, legally recognized line does not always correspond to the forms of sovereignty that prevailed in the Maghreb before colonization. The Sultan’s authority was exercised to varying degrees through relations of allegiance, taxation, religion and political affiliation, without necessarily taking the form of uniform administrative control. It is within this context that Morocco’s claims concerning Ceuta, Melilla and other Spanish territories on the north African coast should be examined.
Following Moroccan independence in 1956, the question of colonial-era borders became a topic of national debate. Moroccan nationalists, particularly Sultan Mohamed V, advocated the recovery of territories considered to have been detached from Morocco during the colonial period. That policy unfolded amid a broader push for decolonization, resulting in Spain relinquishing Tarfaya in 1958 and Sidi Ifni in 1969.
Yet Ceuta and Melilla remained under Spanish control, with the former colonial territories eventually becoming part of the EU’s external border. EU efforts to clamp down on migration in the past few years have transformed the cities, imbuing them with a strategic importance comparable to their historical and military significance.
This change helps explain the paradoxical nature of the Morocco-Spain relationship. Despite strong economic and trade relations, and close cooperation on security and migration, the territorial dispute remains a source of conflict.
In a study of Morocco’s claims to Spanish territories in Africa, the University of Cambridge’s Jamie Trinidad emphasizes that the legal arguments vary for each territory, meaning that Ceuta, Melilla, the Chafarinas Islands and the islet of Perejil are not analogous cases.
However, that does not mean a resolution is out of reach.
Consider Gibraltar, which is frequently invoked in Moroccan political discourse. The process of determining Gibraltar’s status after Brexit, which required close cooperation between the UK, the EU and Spain, demonstrates that a long-standing territorial dispute can end in joint management, even when fundamental positions on sovereignty remain divergent.
That experience offers a lesson for Morocco: Even long-standing territorial disputes can invite cooperation. They can be eased through gradual negotiations, confidence-building measures and other mechanisms that divorce, at least temporarily, questions of sovereignty from the practical necessities of everyday life.
To take such an approach in Ceuta and Melilla would require Europe to recognize that the militarization of borders alone cannot solve the migration issue. They can still be used to exert diplomatic pressure, as recent events have shown. Migration cooperation between Morocco and Spain should be part of a broader strategy focused on economic development, legal mobility, the fight against criminal networks and the protection of fundamental rights.
The future of Ceuta and Melilla should be viewed through the lens of Euro-Mediterranean relations — as sites of dialogue, exchange and cooperation between Africa and Europe, not just fortified borders. Morocco and Spain are fated to coexist. Their geographical proximity, economic and human relations, and shared security interests require a relationship built on trust and mutual respect.
Resolving the territorial dispute will not be easy, as each country has long-standing claims to the two cities, but the time has come to seek a new path based on negotiation, not confrontation.
That would not only mark a new chapter in bilateral relations, but also benefit the wider Mediterranean region.
Moha Ennaji is a professor at Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University.

Officials and lawmakers clash over drone funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:43:11 UTC
01:43:11 KST

Government officials and opposition lawmakers yesterday clashed over funding for uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs), with Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) lawmakers demanding that the regular budget be used for military drones.
KMT lawmakers presented a drone budget plan at a news conference cohosted by the party-affiliated Chung Hsing Policy and Education Foundation at the legislature.
A senior military officer and government officials said that the proposal does not meet urgent national defense needs and would be redundant as an economic policy.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
KMT Legislator Lai Shyh-bao (賴士葆) said that the proposal includes a 40 percent offset for purchases of US drones, meaning that for each drone procured from the US, the suppliers must buy Taiwan-made components worth 40 percent of the contract’s value.
The offset and other measures facilitating technology transfers would ensure growth in the domestic drone industry, which is a crucial goal of the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party, Lai said.
The proposed defense budget for next year is NT$1.1 trillion (US$34.08 billion), or 4 percent of GDP, while the government has previously pledged to increase military spending to 5 percent of GDP, he said.
The massive budget cannot be passed through special funding measures without harming the legislature’s constitutional authority to check the executive branch, he said.
Legislative oversight is a guardrail against waste, especially with rapidly changing drone technologies, Lai said.
Making large orders increases the risk of waste, as UAV models that appear promising at the time of purchase could become obsolete by the time of delivery, he added.
Lieutenant-General Huang Wen-chi (黃文啟), head of the Ministry of National Defense’s Department of Strategic Planning, said that a special drone budget is necessary for obtaining urgently needed capabilities.
“Taiwan is not in a position to freely acquire whatever capabilities it wants,” Huang said.
The military must have the latitude to obtain platforms and systems through alternative means to fill critical capability gaps when regular methods fail to achieve results, Huang said.
Rapidly building domestic UAV manufacturing capability is a crucial national security matter, as Taiwan would most likely be cut off from external supply sources in a conflict with China, he said.
Coastal surveillance drones, attack drones and automated attack boats in the ministry’s special budget are all single-use or otherwise expendable platforms that require constant replacement to be useful, he said.
The armed forces would not be able to begin ramping up drone capabilities without a lot of UAVs to train and operate with, Huang said, adding that time is a crucial factor in national defense.
The drone industry has the potential to become a second strategically valuable economic sector for Taiwan next to chipmaking, a potential the government procurement strategy is not primed to realize, KMT Legislator Huang Chien-hao (黃健豪) said.
The ministry is showing favor to a few manufacturers at the expense of small and medium-sized enterprises (SME), which is not conducive to building supply chains capable of sustaining an industry, he added.
Industry Development Administration Deputy Director-General Chen Kuo-hsuan (陳國軒) said that the government’s drone industry development plan already includes subsidies for SMEs and building domestic supply chains.
Amending laws governing subsidies for the defense industry, SMEs and drones would be more than sufficient to address the opposition’s concerns, Chen said.

Tax revenue remains exceptionally robust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:43:09 UTC
01:43:09 KST

Taiwan’s tax revenue was robust in the first seven months of this year, fueled by a stock-market boom and strong corporate earnings, even as last month’s collections declined because of an unusually high comparison base created by last year’s extended income-tax filing deadline, the Ministry of Finance said yesterday.
Tax revenue was NT$289.1 billion (US$8.96 billion) last month, down 67 percent from a year earlier, the ministry’s data showed.
“The sharp decline was largely a statistical effect rather than a sign of weakening collections,” ministry statistician Liu Shun-rong (劉訓蓉) said.
Photo: CNA
For the first seven months of the year, revenue was NT$2.88 trillion, or 72.9 percent of the full-year budget target, putting collections 15.6 percentage points ahead of the government’s budget schedule, Liu said.
The figures highlight the strength of tax receipts despite the sharp monthly swings, she said.
Securities transaction tax was a key driver in tax revenue last month amid investors’ heavy trading in Taiwanese stocks, fueled by strong demand for artificial intelligence-related companies, the data showed.
Average daily trading turnover on Taiwan’s stock market surged 1.8 times the value of a year earlier to NT$1.15 trillion last month, lifting securities transaction tax revenue 1.7 times to NT$65.1 billion.
For the first seven months, securities transaction tax revenue jumped 1.9 times to NT$398.7 billion, reaching 277 percent of the government’s budget target for the period, the ministry said.
Corporate income tax revenue remained strong, rising 24.1 percent from a year earlier to NT$788.9 billion in the first seven months, mainly reflecting higher tax payments by companies, the ministry said.
Individual income tax revenue increased 11.2 percent to NT$689.9 billion in that same period, it said.
From January to last month, business tax collections climbed 20.8 percent to NT$487.2 billion, helped by steady domestic spending and higher taxes on imports of information and communications technology and audiovisual products, as well as electronic components.
However, land value increment tax revenue was a notable exception, falling 8.5 percent to NT$39.2 billion during the first seven months as property transactions declined, Liu said.
The ministry expects tax revenue to remain elevated this year, supported by strong stock-market turnover and resilient exports from Taiwan’s technology and industrial sectors.

Chinese AI video is coming for more than Hollywood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:43:09 UTC
01:43:09 KST

New large language models (LLM) like Moonshot’s Kimi K3 have dominated the debate about China’s artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions. Yet the clearest evidence of the country’s prowess might be in video and the stakes could extend far beyond just shaking up Hollywood.
Outside of Alphabet Inc’s Google, nearly all of the leading video-generation models are Chinese, making up nine of the top 10 text-to-video systems on benchmarking platform Artificial Analysis’ leaderboard.
ByteDance Ltd and MiniMax Group Inc recently released back-to-back updates to their rival video-generation models. That followed the surprise emergence of Happy Horse, a secretive video system that rattled the industry before being revealed as an Alibaba Group Holding Ltd project. Add Kuaishou Technology’s Kling, Beijing-based ShengShu Technology’s Vidu, as well as a host of other start-ups, and China has developed an unusually crowded roster of major players in a field that US leaders including OpenAI and Anthropic have deprioritized.
Illustration: Mountain People
The tools are increasingly being used by advertising agencies and entertainment studios, and even powered the rise of the fast-growing global microdrama industry. Some view them as a plausible route to revenue in a sector battered by price wars and uncertain business models.
However, their greater strategic significance might be just beginning to emerge. China’s dominance in generative video could give it an advantage in building so-called “world models,” long heralded as the next generation of AI.
Business leaders, backed by a growing body of research, believe that the video tools could end up being the foundation for AI systems that take the technology beyond screens and into the physical world. World models must understand more than just language, also grasping physics and how objects interact with each other in uncertain, real environments. The systems could eventually power humanoid robots or autonomous vehicles.
Some AI pioneers see this as a more viable route to Silicon Valley’s holy grail of artificial general intelligence than building ever-larger chatbots.
To generate convincing video, a model must learn more than aesthetics. It needs at least a rough comprehension of motion, causality and physics, or its outputs can be laughably absurd. As these models scale, researchers have found that rudimentary physical reasoning can emerge even without explicit programming. They still do not understand the world like we do, but they are getting much better at predicting what it should look like and what is likely to happen next. Many researchers are now pairing the video models with instructions to train robots.
Several of China’s leading AI video firms, including ShengShu, are already moving toward releasing world models and broader multimodal systems. It is not just Chinese firms making this connection, either. US-based Runway AI and Germany’s Black Forest Labs, two of the West’s most prominent visual AI start-ups, are following the same trajectory.
Runway chief executive officer Cris Valenzuela told me it is a natural progression. For a video model to be good, it must accurately simulate what you would expect to happen in the real world. A ball rolls through a field rather than glides over it, for example. A robot cannot fold laundry or stock a supermarket merely by recognizing what objects are; it must anticipate what will happen when moves or interacts with them.
The leap from video generation to training world models remains in the early stages, but ever since OpenAI nixed its video tool Sora, Chinese developers have seized the moment and are increasingly setting the pace.
Many challenges remain. Creating video (not to mention world) models require significantly more data and computing resources. Copyright is another vulnerability for the firms. It is a sin the AI industry as a whole has to grapple with, but it has proven harder to hide what is in the training data for video generators compared with chatbots. That has emerged as a major obstacle to Chinese platforms’ overseas expansion efforts.
However, China has already established significant industrial hardware advantages in robotics. Hundreds of firms have figured out how to cobble together a humanoid body; what they still lack is a brain. Increasingly, the data and simulation capabilities developed from video-generation models are being harnessed to build one.
World models might never have a ChatGPT moment. Their strategic importance is unlikely to be demonstrated by a mass consumer tool that millions of users can try for themselves. While Washington has been watching China’s chatbots with growing consternation, it risks focusing on the most visible contest while overlooking progress that might prove more consequential.
Companies and investors should heed the same warning. LLMs continue to absorb most of the capital, but the next breakthrough might come from systems that can navigate the real world rather than just describe it.
If video is the training ground for such machines, China’s early advantages will not stop at just riling up Hollywood. They might determine who leads the next era of AI.
Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

ETF investors continue to increase despite market pullback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:43:03 UTC
01:43:03 KST

Taiwanese investors stepped up regular monthly purchases of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) last month despite a sharp market pullback, suggesting that they viewed the volatility as a buying opportunity rather than a reason to retreat from equities, Taiwan Depository and Clearing Corp (TDCC, 台灣集中保管結算所) data showed.
The number of investors making regular purchases of ETFs increased 1.24 million last month from the previous month, TDCC data showed. So far this year, the figure has grown by 6.37 million, the data showed.
Of the 94 ETFs listed in Taiwan, investors in Yuanta/P-shares Taiwan Top 50 ETF (0050) rose by the most of 324,400, followed by Capital Taiex Daily Leveraged 2X ETF (00685L) by 185,700 and Yuanta/P-shares Taiwan Dividend Plus ETF (0056) by 91,200, the data showed.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
The resilience of regular ETF investing highlights how the strategy has gained traction among retail investors. By investing a fixed amount regularly, investors gain more ETF units when prices fall, potentially lowering their average purchase cost over time.
Among the 10 most widely held ETFs, Capital Taiwan Growth ETF (00981A) posted the strongest return so far this year, gaining 76.29 percent including dividends, the data showed.
Cathay Taiwan Technology Leaders ETF (00881) ranked second with a 74.28 percent return, while Fubon Technology ETF (0052), which has a heavy weighting in Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), gained 64.42 percent, the data showed.
The two major market-cap-weighted ETFs — Yuanta/P-shares Taiwan Top 50 ETF (0050) and Fubon FTSE TWSE Taiwan 50 (006208) — also delivered remarkable returns of more than 60 percent. By comparison, Capital Taiwan Selected High Dividend ETF (00919), a favorite among income-focused investors, posted a return of 43.57 percent year to date, the data showed.
The performance gap reflects a market increasingly driven by artificial-intelligence (AI) demand, as technology-heavy ETFs have benefited from sharp gains in Taiwan’s semiconductor and other technology stocks, while high-dividend funds generally have less exposure to some of the market’s strongest-performing growth shares.
Taiwan Stock Exchange said ETFs with heavier technology exposure have benefited disproportionately from the AI boom, while dividend-focused products have offered a different balance of income and diversification.
Still, the strong year-to-date gains of many ETFs provided a cushion against last month’s market pullback. For investors using regular monthly plans, the decline may have made ETFs even more attractive by allowing them to accumulate more units at lower prices, the exchange said.
Overall, the continued growth in regular ETF investment suggests that retail investors are increasingly treating the funds as a core vehicle for long-term equity exposure, and many appear willing to stay invested and use price declines to build their holdings rather than abandoning the market during periods of volatility, it said.

The back-to-school blues are here — for parents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:43:02 UTC
01:43:02 KST

School in the US does not begin again for a few weeks, but you would not know it looking at my phone. These days, returning to the classroom seems to involve more homework for parents than for students.
Weeks before my child has been assigned a teacher or seen a syllabus, we are fielding an invite for a weekend kindergarten campout. We are buying new school shoes and uniforms. Signing up for piano, dance and baseball. And do not forget end-of-summer grade-level parties. And new class welcome parties. And the evening events for parents.
I am sure my children will easily start waking up at 6:45am again.
Is anyone else ready to cry uncle? No? Everyone else is doing OK?
Me too, of course.
Don’t get me wrong. The rhythm of the school year promises a structure and a schedule that I cherish and miss in the chaos of summer. It brings friends and community back together after summer’s separate ways.
However, the transition brings its share of stress, too.
Wondering if this is just American madness, I asked my new British friends if they find parenting and school schedules this intense. I was both frustrated and relieved to hear them say: “Yes.”
They too have Pajama Day and Crazy Socks Day. They too face homework projects that consume much more parental time than that of the student — printing off ancient photographs to help a kindergartener make an elaborate family tree. They too have wine moms (“mums”) and midcareer mothers trying to juggle corporate travel and school snacks.
In other words, there is no escaping the hustle that is modern parenting.
It has me wishing two things:
First, I desperately wish we could call a collective truce and agree that less is more. Enough of the arms race of parties and get-togethers, and “fun” activities that involve the parents as much as the children. I love my children, really I do, but when they are at school, can they be at school without parental involvement, save for a spring recital?
Second, if we are going to put this much energy into school, might we instead put it into academic rigor? Over the years, very little of the parental stress I have experienced around the return to school is about academics. And I’m not saying this because my children are acing every class.
In my experience, much of the school hustle is not about learning. It is more about logistics — school events, coordinating schedules, social obligations and figuring out how, amid it all, the children will get carted to and fro.
Meanwhile, math levels in the US have dropped to a near two-decade low. Reading levels have fallen back to 1992 levels, according to the US National Assessment of Educational Progress, widely called “the nation’s report card.”
I would trade Spirit Week for more time spent reading full books, more spelling bees and math drills, and earlier language immersion.
After all, that is what school is for: children’s education.
When did it start feeling like it is more about project management for the parents?
I cannot remember my own parents setting foot on school grounds for anything other than a spring concert or an open house. They did not manage group texts, sign up for weekend campouts or go to school auctions. They did not need to monitor homework — first and foremost because it was not on a screen connected to the Internet so we could do it alone in our rooms.
No wonder, according to the Pew Research Center, 62 percent of parents believe that parenting is more difficult than they thought it would be.
Perhaps, 11 years into my parenting journey, I have developed a case of senioritis. I am forever grateful to our dear school and the brave souls who volunteered as this year’s room reps. I know I should probably buy classroom birthday gifts in bulk to keep in a closet like I keep meaning to. Because when just about every child in the grade is going to have a birthday party and invite the entire class, and you have three kids, that is at least 75 parties. Add that to the back-to-school prep list, which already runs the average American family about US$900.
As a student, I always loved an honors program, but as a mother? Please, I will take a pass on the extra homework.
Abby McCloskey is a columnist, podcast host and consultant. She directed domestic policy on two presidential campaigns and was director of economic policy at the American Enterprise Institute. Academic integrity, AI ethics should be in schools: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

Academic integrity and artificial intelligence (AI) ethics should be incorporated as core teaching content, as nearly half of surveyed students did not understand rules and ethics regarding AI use, student group EdYouth said yesterday.
The organization presented its fifth 2019 curriculum observation report, which seeks to understand students’ views of how the curriculum is being implemented. The latest report was the first on science and social science subjects.
The report included data on academic integrity education, digital learning platform observations and what affects students’ choices of school clubs, as well as information on arts education, local languages, psychiatric consultation and vocational education.
Photo: CNA
Taiwanese schools do not have a standalone course for academic integrity, and nearly one-quarter of respondents said no one had taught them about it, said National Chengchi University second-year student Chen Yin-chia (陳胤嘉), one of the main authors of the report.
Despite the Ministry of Education warning students about the use of generative AI, nearly half of respondents said they “did not understand” or were “very confused” regarding regulations on the technology.
Deputy Minister of Education Chu Chun-chang (朱俊彰) said the ministry would work with students to expand their ability to conduct logical arguments, develop empathy, focus on teamwork and include courses on academic integrity.
The ministry has been studying what AI could do for students and to the educational field, and in May proposed a road map on how to develop students’ ability to use AI responsibly, for learning and to resolve issues, while cultivating abilities and skill sets that cannot be substituted by AI, Chu said.
Four students from Taipei, New Taipei City, Changhua County and Taitung County said that if students “outsource” their thought processes to AI, they risk becoming passive learners.
That would make it difficult to realize the core competencies emphasized by the curriculum, such as independent action and interactive communication, they said.
The course would help stimulate critical thinking, media literacy and public participation, the students said.
Two students from Kaohsiung and Hualien County said that students need to learn what should be left to AI and what can be done by themselves, and why there should be such distinctions.
The students suggested that curricula around AI be standardized, and that courses to understand AI limitations should be introduced into the national curriculum.

Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) yesterday lambasted Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅?萁) for failing to attend cross-caucus negotiations and suggested that Fu step down from the position if he continued to miss meetings.
The Legislative Yuan yesterday afternoon met to discuss this fiscal year’s general budget.
Han had expressed his intent to pass the budget by Friday last week, but the deadline passed without consensus, with more than 100 proposals still pending review.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
Fu was absent from cross-
caucus negotiations on July 30, July 31, Tuesday last week, Thursday last week and yesterday.
After confirming that both Democratic Progressive Party caucus whip Tsai Chi-chang (蔡其昌) and Taiwan People’s Party caucus whip Chen Ching-lung (陳清龍) were present, Han asked the KMT caucus whether Fu would attend the meeting.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
The answer was important, as Fu’s absence would mean that the other whips’ presence at the meeting were for naught, he said.
When KMT caucus secretary-general Lin Pei-hsiang (林沛祥) said Fu was not attending, Han asked Lin if he was authorized to vote on the KMT caucus’ behalf.
Han posed the same question to Chen and Tsai, both of whom stated that in the event of their absence, the signature of their deputies would represent the caucus.
Lin said that while he was authorized to sign any agreements, his signature could not represent the caucus.
Han said that the attempts of one caucus leader to micromanage proceedings have rendered the legislature dysfunctional and showed that he has little regard for the speaker, other caucuses and officials.
“You tell Fu, right now, that he has three choices: come in person, which he should have done; continue to be absent, but fully authorize you to make a decision; or quit his position as whip,” Han told Lin.
The legislature is duty-bound to ensure that the nation continues to improve, that the government can govern more efficiently without corruption and that the public can live a better life, Han said.
“We are not here to be bombastic because we hold a title,” he added.
Later, when it was time to sign the conclusions of the meeting, the KMT caucus initially withheld its signature, prompting Han to lose his temper again and say: "The legislature has been taken over by dark forces."
The caucuses eventually reached a consensus to put the general budget bill to a vote at a plenary session on Friday.
If it does not clear its third reading, an additional plenary session would be convened on Friday next week.
In a statement released last night, Fu said that his absence was by no means a sign of disrespect toward Han or the other party caucuses, but rather that he "could not bear to see Han subjected to various indignities by the Executive Yuan."
Regarding the general budget, Fu confirmed that Han requested that opposition lawmakers to reduce their number of motions to about 100.
Communications among opposition lawmakers are aimed at finalizing this reduction so that the review of the general budget can be completed on schedule, he added.
A source commenting on condition of anonymity said that the split between Han and Fu began when Han ran for speaker in 2024.
Fu intended to campaign as deputy speaker, but Han approached Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) for the position, the source said.
Han was also displeased that Fu staged boycotts in the legislature without informing him, they added.
The divide widened on July 29, when Fu was allegedly displeased with Han’s request for the opposition parties to reduce the number of budget cuts to 60 by the day of the vote.
Han berating Fu might be the first time the legislature has seen a speaker openly criticize a fellow party member, the source said.

Colombia scrambles to find survivors as quake kills 169
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:57 UTC
01:42:57 KST

Colombian volunteers and rescuers yesterday cleared rubble with their bare hands to search for survivors after the country’s strongest earthquake in a decade killed at least 169 people and smashed dozens of buildings.
The magnitude 7.4 quake struck cities across Colombia’s western region shortly after 7:30am on Monday, sending panicked residents onto the streets.
The quake killed 169 people and injured more than 600, according to an association of Colombian city mayors. The deaths were concentrated in Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdo. The mayors also reported that 165 buildings collapsed.
Photo: AFP
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella — just three days after being sworn into the job — declared a state of emergency and vowed a concerted rescue effort.
Pereira, which was among those hit hardest, was mostly plunged into darkness amid power outages on Monday night, as volunteers probed for signs of life under collapsed buildings.
“We’re without power. This seems honestly like a zombie city,” resident Juan David Gaitan said.
Photo: AP
Tattoo artist Andres Hernandez said he was worried about his family and friends, adding that he would stay awake because structures around him were “on the verge of collapsing.”
Hernandez recalled being asleep at home when the quake happened and rushing into the street for safety, as the quake devastated the city in the heart of Colombia’s coffee-growing region.
“It was a movie scene, because I saw the poles, the cables, everything moving. I’m worried about my family, my friends,” he said.
There were scenes of destruction in several cities, with furniture and fabrics sandwiched between concrete walls, floors tossed into irregular angles and cables strewn across roads.
In Manizales, the quake crumpled a tower of the city’s famous neo-Gothic cathedral.
In Quibdo, the capital of Colombia’s Choco department, local official Jenny Rivas said public services and communications “have been virtually shut down.”
“People ran out naked, people jumped from the second floor of their homes,” Quibdo resident and law student Wilmer Cuesta said.
Dentist Julian Pena said he “ran outside carrying nothing” after feeling strong tremors and found hundreds doing the same.
“People were praying in the street. It was overwhelming,” he said.
“There are many buildings with gaps, with cracks. There are others that have completely collapsed.”
The quake was felt across Colombia, including the capital, Bogota, where crowds rushed out into the street in their pajamas.
At a depth of 110km, the quake was also felt in Ecuador and Panama.
Experts at the US Geological Survey said the quake was likely caused by movement along a deep fault within the Nazca tectonic plate.
Hospitals in five Colombian cities were put on red alert on Monday and a nighttime curfew was declared in Cali, local authorities said.
At least six local airports suspended operations, the civil aeronautics agency said.
The devastation comes less than two months after powerful twin quakes rattled neighboring Venezuela, killing more than 6,300 people and leaving tens of thousands homeless.
Messages of support came in from countries across the region and the world.
Pope Leo XIV is “deeply saddened” and “raises his prayers to the Lord for the prompt recovery of those affected by this tragedy,” the Vatican said yesterday.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday said the US was “closely monitoring” the situation and “stands ready to support the people of Colombia.”
The US announced US$15.5 million in emergency relief.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU had mobilized Copernicus, a satellite service, to help with rescue operations.
Israel, Mexico, Ecuador and France also offered assistance.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) diplomacy task force on Sunday signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the European Values Center for Security Policy in Chiayi County.
Chiang Zhen-wei (江振瑋), head of the task force, and Marketa Pekarova Adamova, global advisory board member for the center, signed the MOU after attending the Taiwan-Czech Republic-Ukraine Battlefield Experimentation Workshop at the Asian UAV AI Innovation Application R&D Center in Puzih City (朴子).
The Chiayi County Government, the task force and the Czech Republic-based Farpoint Academy hosted the event from Monday to Friday last week.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Twenty-two experts from the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology, the Institute for National Defense and Security Research and other institutions attended the workshop.
The ministry said it hopes to use such events to cultivate its own seed instructors to serve in the Diplomatic Allies Prosperity Project, which it established to “deepen substantive relations with allies and like-minded countries.”
Chiang told the event that drone diplomacy uses the “chip diplomacy” strategy, with the goal to expand Taiwan’s influence by leveraging industries in which the nation excels.
Taiwan’s drone manufacturing capabilities, semiconductor components provision capacity and its place in the non-China production chain highlight the nation’s importance and favor its increased collaboration in drone development with like-minded nations, he said.
Adamova said she had spoken with Chiang many times when visiting the UAV center and was glad to see Taiwan and the academy collaborate on drones.
Hopefully the MOU will be the basis for deeper Czech-Taiwan drone collaboration, she said.
The ministry said the task force has signed deals with the US, Japan and other countries, while also facilitating projects with like-minded partners in Europe.
It would continue to support its drone diplomatic initiative to foster a secure, resilient and prosperous drone supply chain, it said.

70 dead, 204 roads blocked: Himachal Pradesh reels under monsoon fury; damage tops Rs 910 crore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:42:54 UTC
01:42:54 KST

TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 11, 2026, 22:16 IST

Small

Car lies damaged after falling rocks and debris from a hillside hit it following continuous heavy rainfall in the Anni area of Kullu
Heavy monsoon rains continued to disrupt life across Himachal Pradesh, with 204 roads blocked, 70 people killed in rain-related incidents and damage to public property estimated at more than Rs 910 crore over the past 43 days, according to the latest State Emergency Operation Centre (SEOC) assessment.The assessment covers the period from June 30 to August 11 and captures the impact of repeated heavy rainfall, landslides, cloudbursts and other weather-related incidents across the hill state.
70 disaster deaths, public property damage crosses Rs 910 crore
According to SEOC data, 70 people have died in direct disaster-related incidents since June 30. Landslides accounted for 14 deaths, while 23 people died after falling from steep slopes, rocks or trees. Seven deaths were caused by snake bites, six by electrocution and four by cloudbursts.Lahaul and Spiti reported the highest number of direct disaster-related deaths at 14, followed by Kangra with 12.The wider toll has also been compounded by road accidents. As many as 93 people have died in road accidents during the same period, with Chamba reporting 16 fatalities, followed by Kullu (13), Sirmaur (12) and Shimla (11), as reproted by ANI.Meanwhile, cumulative damage to public property has reached around Rs 910.35 crore.
The Public Works Department has suffered the biggest losses, estimated at Rs 686.36 crore, while damage to the power sector stands at around Rs 203.90 crore.The monsoon has also damaged houses, other private structures, livestock and crops across the state's 12 districts, adding to losses for affected households.
204 roads blocked, power and water infrastructure hit
Mandi is the worst affected in terms of road connectivity, with 80 roads currently blocked. The Mandi-Kullu route has also been disrupted at Jalogi Dwada. Kullu has reported 56 blocked roads, while 23 roads remain closed in Sirmaur. Two national highways — NH-154 and NH-21 — are also among the affected routes.The road closures have disrupted inter-district connectivity and complicated the movement of essential supplies and emergency response teams.
The monsoon has also damaged the state's power and drinking water infrastructure. Forty-five distribution transformer regions are currently out of service, including 41 in Sirmaur's Nahan subdivision.Around 82 drinking water supply schemes have been affected across the state. Sirmaur accounts for 31 of the disrupted schemes, followed by Hamirpur with 11 and Mandi with eight.Authorities and emergency response teams are continuing restoration work, including clearing landslides and debris, reopening roads and restoring power and water supply. However, persistent rainfall and the risk of further landslides continue to hamper relief and restoration efforts.

Machinery exports for July grew almost 20%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:52 UTC
01:42:52 KST

The nation’s machinery exports grew 18.4 percent year-on-year to US$3.305 billion last month, the 18th consecutive monthly increase, the Taiwan Association of Machinery Industry reported on Monday.
The increase was lifted mainly by shipments of electronic equipment, which grew 35.6 percent to US$709.5 million, amid strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications and semiconductors, the association said in a report.
Machine tools posted an 8.8 percent increase from a year earlier, but their shipments of US$178 million were relatively low compared with other product categories, as the New Taiwan dollar exchange rate was unfavorable for Taiwanese firms’ competitiveness, it said.
Photo: EPA
Overall, Taiwan’s machinery exports in the first seven months of this year reached US$21.101 billion, up 19.1 percent from a year earlier, while machine tool shipments fell 1.5 percent to US$1.156 billion during the same period, association data showed.
The US remained the largest buyer of Taiwanese machinery products in the first seven months, with purchases worth US$5.439 billion, accounting for 25.8 percent of exports.
China ranked second, with purchases of US$4.453 billion for a 21.1 percent share of exports. Singapore followed with purchases of US$1.587 billion and accounting for 7.5 percent of the total, the data showed.
Taiwan’s machinery industry has maintained steady growth at the start of the second half of the year, as strong demand for semiconductors and AI servers boosted shipments of electronic equipment and inspection and testing equipment, the association said.
However, political issues and regulatory policies in some countries, such as high-tech and rare earth controls, have gradually impacted global supply chains and could weigh on Taiwanese manufacturers’ order visibility and export outlook, which warrants further observation, it said.

Chinese immigrant Xu Chunying (徐春鶯) was yesterday sentenced for campaigning for political candidates at the behest of Chinese agents, making her the ninth person, including elected officials and candidates, to be sentenced to prison for collaborating with Beijing since the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法) was promulgated in 2020.
The legislation, aimed at preventing hostile foreign powers from interfering with elections, was passed in 2019 and enacted the following year.
Xu yesterday became the most recent public figure to be sentenced under the act after the New Taipei District Court handed her seven years in prison for campaigning on behalf of Chinese agents, among other offenses.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
The Supreme Court last month upheld a guilty verdict against Lin Hsueh-feng (林雪峰), a former Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chiayi City councilor candidate, who is serving a four-year sentence.
Lin was charged over taking borough wardens and potential voters on Beijing-funded trips to China starting in 2023.
Chinese officials hosted those on the trips at banquets and gave speeches on who to vote for in the general election the following year, court documents showed.
Ma Chih-wei (馬治薇), a former independent legislative candidate who in 2023 passed classified information to China in exchange for campaign contributions, was sentenced to two years and eight months in prison.
Ma was found guilty of leaking lists of names of Criminal Investigation Bureau and National Security Bureau officials, and other central government personnel, as well as political intelligence.
Gong He Party Chairman Chou Ke-chi (周克琦), and Taipei Puxian Association board members Chu Chun-yuan (朱俊源) and Pan Jindong (潘進東) rallied for the party’s Taipei mayoral and city councilor candidates in the 2022 election after receiving funds from the provincial government of China’s Fujian.
The High Court this year upheld the guilty verdicts for the three, who were sentenced to terms of one to two years.
Borough wardens were also accused of taking people on trips funded by Chinese officials.
Court records showed that most of the Chinese Communist Party officials explicitly told the visitors to support the KMT or the Taiwan People’s Party.
Yao Wei-hua (姚韋華), a borough warden in New Taipei City’s Tucheng District (土城), and Chien An-shih (簡安仕), chairman of a China cultural exchange group, were originally found not guilty of arranging Beijing-funded trips to China in 2023 for five other borough wardens and nine friends.
The High Court earlier this year reversed the verdict.
Yao faces four years and eight months in prison, while Chien faces two years and six months, although the verdicts are not final.

“Saint Vincent and the Grenadines was still a young nation when we started our relationship on Aug. 15, 1981, having gained political independence less than two years prior,” he said.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
Reflecting on the decades of ties, Friday said the two countries had become more than friends.
“We are partners in a world that is yet to enable Taiwan to contribute fully to international forums and in vital organizations,” he said.
He thanked Taiwan for investing in his country and people over the past 45 years.
Friday also pledged his government’s continued support for Taiwan’s bid to participate in international forums, including the UN and its specialized agencies, as well as organizations such as Interpol.
Marking the anniversary, Friday said his new government had identified four pillars for economic development: agriculture, tourism, the blue economy and the new economy.
The blue economy includes fisheries, marinas and other maritime industries, while the new economy includes sports, the creative industries, entertainment and information technology, he said.
“Saint Vincent and the Grenadines welcomes investors in every sector, particularly those that I just mentioned,” he said, adding that even modest investment “can go a long way to creating more opportunities and providing good jobs for our people.”
“I am ready to work with you to write the next chapter of this 45-year relationship. I am prepared for partnership,” he said.
Lai welcomed Friday with a military honors ceremony in front of the Presidential Office that included a 21-gun salute.
The president thanked Friday for choosing Taiwan as his first overseas destination since taking office eight months ago, saying the decision demonstrated the two countries’ “staunch and robust diplomatic ties” to the international community.
Lai said Taiwan was “deeply moved” by Saint Vincent and Grenadines’ steadfast support for its international participation and valued the friendship between the two countries as they marked the anniversary of diplomatic relations.
“Looking ahead, Taiwan will continue to deepen cooperation with Saint Vincent and the Grenadines across all sectors. Through a diverse range of programs, we can continue to enhance the welfare of both our peoples,” Lai said.
Friday and his delegation arrived in Taiwan early yesterday for a five-day visit that concludes on Saturday.
Friday is to attend events marking the anniversary of diplomatic relations and participate in an investor roundtable bringing together the Vincentian delegation and prospective Taiwanese investors, the two governments said.

EDITORIAL: Energy infrastructure in the AI era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

Taiwan aims to align with global energy trends by proposing to require heavy industrial power users build dedicated power-generation capacity or install energy-storage systems, a critical step in the nation’s efforts to bolster power resilience and safeguard supply stability amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
The legislature’s Economics Committee last week gave preliminary approval to a draft amendment to the Energy Administration Act (能源管理法) that would require large energy users — such as semiconductor companies, data center operators, steelmakers and petrochemical companies — to build on-site power plants or energy-storage systems for new factories or capacity extensions at existing factories. Limited land availability was a major factor in the government’s decision to narrow the amendment’s scope, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said, dismissing environmentalists’ concerns that the change would hinder efforts to optimize power-use efficiency.
In the US, the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge commits leading hyperscalers and AI companies, including Meta and Microsoft, to buy or develop the additional energy generation required for their data centers and to pay for the grid infrastructure, rather than passing that burden on to other energy customers. Comparable, but not identical, constraints are emerging in Ireland and Singapore. The Netherlands tightly restricts hyperscale siting and imposes severe grid-capacity constraints on new projects.
The proposed rules arrive as AI demand causes unprecedented strain on public electricity grids worldwide. Taiwan manufactures the majority of the advanced chips powering AI data centers, and the complex processes and specialized components used to make those chips are highly power-intensive. The nation’s power consumption is expected to grow at an average annual rate of 2.5 percent from this year through 2035, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said in June, much higher than the 1.7 percent average annual growth forecast for the period from last year to 2034. The ministry attributed the change to surging power demand as a result of economic growth, semiconductor industry expansions, data centers and AI, as well as rising temperatures.
Adding to energy concerns, the nighttime reserve margin is expected to remain below the 15 percent benchmark from this year through 2029, falling to 7.1 percent, indicating that electricity supply would be tight, the ministry said, adding that supply pressure has been shifting toward nighttime.
To limit massive power consumption by large data centers, Taiwan Power Co (Taipower) has for nearly three years suspended new power connectors for data centers with capacity of 5 megawatts (MW) or more in Taoyuan and areas to its north. Taoyuan is already home to data centers, including AI facilities, while some are under construction or planned there. The restriction was conditionally eased last month, with some data centers permitted in designated areas. The relaxation came after Taipower added gas-fired units to the Datan Power Plant in Taoyuan’s Guanyin District (觀音), as well as a power plant redevelopment in Keelung.
Details of the proposed energy regulations would remain unclear until implementing regulations are issued, which the ministry said it expects to do within six months of the amendment passing the legislature. Hundreds of companies would be subject to the new rules, the economics ministry said. It said it is considering defining “heavy energy users” based on renewable energy obligations under the Renewable Energy Development Act (再生能源發展條例) and related regulations. In other words, those with Taipower electricity contracts of at least 5MW would be considered heavy power consumers and required to install power plants or energy storage equipment for new factories.
That threshold should be uncontroversial, but local manufacturers have voiced concerns about the size of dedicated energy capacity and how quickly they must meet the requirement. The ministry said it could follow the rules of the Renewable Energy Development Act and request that large power users obtain 10 percent of the 5MW from their own power plants initially and increase the ratio gradually. Additionally, what kind of power plants should they build? All of those considerations need to be factored into their cost structure.
The ministry must work with heavy energy users to establish a feasible schedule, or little would be achieved. Given the costs of power plants, energy storage systems and land acquisition, some companies might consider paying the fines of NT$150,000 to NT$750,000, but repeated fines could add up.
The phrase “at sixes and sevens” refers to being in a state of disarray. How telling it is that the two numbers had a special significance for the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) last week. The TPP was formally established on Aug. 6, 2019. Thursday was its seventh anniversary and it marked the event at the party’s annual national congress meeting in Taichung on Sunday last week. It was also the week that the latest My Formosa public opinion poll was released, showing that the TPP’s approval rating had fallen 6 percentage points since the beginning of the year. The dip in public

Google’s AI team hesitates to use its own HR filter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

Alphabet Inc’s Google pitches its artificial intelligence (AI) tools to corporate clients as a way to more quickly sift through a mountain of job applications to find the most promising candidates — but some of its own AI researchers do not want to rely on these tools when recruiting.
Google DeepMind’s AGI Safety and Alignment Team, which seeks to mitigate the risks of advanced AI, is encouraging job candidates for its open roles to fill out a special form alongside their application to eliminate the risk it might be automatically screened out by the company’s internal AI systems, according to a document viewed by Bloomberg, which contained the disclaimer “PLEASE DO NOT SHARE THIS DOC WIDELY.”
“We have an applications system with a non-trivial probability your CV will be screened out incorrectly or take too long to reach us,” the document states. “Filling out this form makes sure that a real human on the team will get to see your application.”
Photo: Bloomberg
A Google DeepMind spokesperson said the company aims to “recruit and hire the most qualified talent at Google DeepMind” and denied that the company’s systems filter out applicants incorrectly.
“This team set up a special form to go past the recruiter review, and get their resumes direct to the people on the team. But there are no shortcuts to getting hired,” the spokesperson added.
AI has rapidly become a part of the hiring process, prompting some human resources (HR) teams to worry they might soon be out of a job. But how that AI is employed can be murky. Some companies run AI models to rank applicants, while others filter resumes for key terms.
Google’s Workspace team, which sells popular products such as Google Drive to businesses, markets the company’s new AI features as a way to “save HR time by quickly creating drafts for job postings, evaluating resumes, and forecasting hiring needs.”
AI hiring systems have also come under fire for potentially discriminating against candidates. A Bloomberg investigation found that OpenAI’s ChatGPT showed signs of potential bias based on applicants’ names.
Workday Inc, which sells workplace management software, is facing a lawsuit that alleges its AI hiring systems screen applicants based on race, age and disability in violation of the law. Workday has denied the allegations and said humans make hiring decisions. The company did not respond to an additional request for comment.
Meanwhile, some job candidates are using AI to their advantage by gaming the filters, or simply churning out applications in record time. The Google DeepMind team was on guard about this possibility as well, counseling candidates that their applications would be stronger without the help of AI.
The form designed to circumvent automated screening includes an advisory: “A real human will read these. These humans get really tired of reading LLM answers, because they all sound very samey.”

ENGLISH DIGEST 實用美語(空中美語)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:47 UTC
01:42:47 KST

As the July sun beats down on Taiwan, the heat inevitably pushes us toward lightweight T-shirts. Interestingly, thousands of years ago, the ancient Greeks lived under similar skies and also dressed for the weather.
Around the bright Aegean Sea, the ancient Greeks favored the air circulation and freedom of movement provided by loose clothing. In summer, they preferred breathable linen that felt light against the skin. Clothes were usually made at home by women or household servants. They first wove rectangular lengths of cloth to the required size. Then, with draping, pins and a belt, these plain lengths became elegant, practical outfits.
From this way of wearing cloth emerged three classic styles that are still known today. The first of these was the “chiton,” an everyday tunic, fastened with pins at the shoulders and belted at the waist. Worn by both genders, it was often knee-length for men and ankle-length for women. The “peplos,” a floor-length piece of clothing usually worn by women, had a folded top that created a neat, layered look. For outdoor wear, people added a “himation,” a wide wrap that could offer shade or extra warmth.
Photo: Freepik / 照片：Freepik
However, ancient Greek fashion wasn’t merely about surviving the climate. It reflected deeper cultural values. They valued balance and proportion, so balanced draping reflected their sense of beauty and order. Meanwhile, fabric quality, border designs and skilled draping conveyed social rank. That’s why wealthy citizens wore finer wool and fabrics colored with costly purple dyes, while workers relied on coarser, undyed fabric.
Today, this aesthetic still dominates fashion shows and red carpets. Those flowing goddess-style gowns celebrities love are modern heirs of ancient Greek draped fashion. Ancient Greek clothing teaches us that great style isn’t necessarily about elaboration. In summer especially, with simple fabric and smart draping, suddenly, the heat feels easier to bear.
當七月的太陽炙烤著臺灣時，高溫不可避免地把我們推向輕薄的 T 恤。有趣的是，數千年前，古希臘人生活在相似的天空下，也會因應氣候來穿著。
在明亮的愛琴海周圍，古希臘人偏好寬鬆衣物所帶來的空氣流通和活動自由。在夏天，他們偏好透氣的亞麻布，穿起來輕盈且親膚。衣服通常由女性或家中僕人在家製作。他們先將長方形的布匹織成所需的尺寸。接著，透過垂墜掛法、別針和一條腰帶，這些樸素的布料就變成優雅且實用的服裝。
從這種穿衣方式中出現了三種至今仍為人所知的經典款式。其中第一種是「chiton」，一種日常束腰外衣，在雙肩用別針固定並在腰間繫腰帶。男女都會穿著這種服裝，男款通常是及膝長度，女款則是及踝長度。「peplos」則是一種通常由女性穿著的及地服飾，上方有反折設計，營造出整齊且具層次感的視覺效果。至於外出穿著，人們會加上一件「himation」，它是一種寬大的披巾，可以提供遮蔭或額外的保暖。
然而，古希臘的時尚不僅僅是為了適應氣候。它反映了更深層的文化價值。他們重視平衡與比例，因此平衡的垂褶展現出他們對美與秩序的感知。同時，布料品質、滾邊設計以及精湛的垂褶技藝傳達了社會地位。這就是為什麼富有的公民會穿較細緻的羊毛，以及用昂貴紫色染料染成的面料，而勞動者則依賴較粗糙、未經染色的布料。
如今，這種美學仍然主導著時裝秀和紅毯。那些名人喜愛的飄逸女神風長禮服正是古希臘垂褶時尚的現代傳承。古希臘服裝告訴我們，出色的風格未必需要繁複的設計。尤其在夏天，只要簡單的布料和巧妙的垂褶，炎熱就會頓時變得比較容易忍受。
KEY VOCABULARY
1. inevitably adv. 不可避免地；必然地
If you keep eating junk food every day, you will inevitably gain weight.
如果你每天都吃垃圾食物，你將無法避免變胖。
2. linen n. 亞麻布；亞麻製品
This shirt is made of linen, so it feels cool on hot summer days.
這件襯衫是亞麻布做的，所以在炎熱的夏天穿起來很涼爽。
3. outfit n. 服裝；裝備
Sandra is so fashionable. She always wears the cutest outfits at school.
珊卓真時髦！她在學校總是穿著最可愛的服裝。
4. fasten v. 固定；繫牢
Patty pulled her hair back away from her face and fastened it with a hair clip.
派蒂把頭髮從臉上往後撥並用髮夾固定。
5. proportion n. 比例；部分
The proportion of students pursuing science degrees has increased significantly over the past decade.
過去十年中，攻讀科學學位的學生比例顯著增加。
6. coarse adj. 粗糙的；粗魯的
The farmer wore coarse gloves to protect his hands while working.
那位農夫在工作時戴著粗糙的手套來保護雙手。
7. dominate v. 占首要地位；統治
Issues relating to the recent refugee crisis dominated the presidential debate.
關於最近難民危機的議題主導了總統選舉的辯論。
8. celebrity n. 名人；明星
It’s these people’s job to follow celebrities and take lots of photos of them.
這些人的工作是跟蹤名人並拍下許多他們的照片。
9. heir n. 繼承人
Lydia is heir to her family’s large fortune and extensive business interests.
莉迪亞是她家族鉅額財富和龐大商業利益的繼承人。
MORE INFORMATION

the Aegean (Sea) 愛琴海
breathable adj. 透氣的
drape v. 指布料或衣服自然垂掛，形成垂褶
（分詞 draping 多指布料垂墜或披掛的方式， draped 則形容具有垂墜感的）

Compal Electronics Inc (仁寶電腦) yesterday said it expects artificial intelligence (AI) servers to account for 30 to 40 percent of revenue next year, up from about 10 percent this year, as it expands production capacity in Taiwan, the US and Vietnam.
In the first quarter, server revenue was NT$10 billion (US$309.8 million), accounting for 5 percent of the company’s revenue, Compal chairman Ray Chen (陳瑞聰) told reporters as the company inaugurated its new plant in Taoyuan.
“We are targeting triple-digit annual growth for our AI-related business this year and next year,” Chen said.
Photo: CNA
The new plant would serve as a key site for Compal’s AI server research, development and production, featuring fully automated production lines for Level 10 (L10) AI server systems and Level 11 (L11) server racks, Chen said.
It should start contributing revenue from next quarter, he said.
Amid strong demand for AI servers, Compal expects the new plant to reach full utilization as early as the second half of next year, Chen said.
The company is evaluating AI server capacity expansion in Taoyuan, although the location and scale have yet to be determined, he added.
Compal’s AI server business remains focused on L10 products, with shipments mainly to neocloud customers such as GMI Cloud and Verda, while L11 shipments are slated to begin next quarter, he said.
Alongside expansion in Taiwan, Compal is increasing AI server capacity in Vietnam and Texas, Chen said.
In Vietnam, where Compal mainly handles Level 6 (L6) server node production, the company operates four surface-mount technology lines and plans to add another six, with construction of its second factory nearing completion, he said.
Compal is building two plants in Taylor and Georgetown, Texas, focused on the production of L6, L10 and L11 models. Trial production is slated to begin next quarter, followed by mass production in the first quarter of next year, Chen said.
The company had planned to ship some L6 products from Vietnam to Texas for assembly, but is adding L6 capacity in Texas as some US customers seek more localized production, he said.
The move would allow Compal to handle production from L6 through L11 rack-level integration in Texas, he said.
The Texas plants would mainly serve US hyperscalers and enterprise customers, while Taiwan primarily serves neocloud customers, Chen said.
The PC industry faces headwinds this year from tight DRAM supply and rising component costs, with International Data Corp forecasting global PC shipments to fall 10 to 12 percent year-on-year.
Chen said DRAM supply is likely to remain tight next year, but rising component costs are pushing up average selling prices, meaning Compal’s PC revenue might not fall at the same pace as shipments.

Two Chinese suspected to have illegally entered Taiwan are being held incommunicado, the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) said yesterday, after a rubber boat was found north of the Port of Taipei last month.
An angler late last month discovered a rubber boat on a beach in New Taipei City’s Bali District (八里), a member of the public wrote on Threads on Monday.
The next day, the angler investigated the boat and discovered that it contained Chinese-made metal oil drums, toilet paper packaging with simplified Chinese characters, an empty soda bottle sold in China and three life jackets, the post said.
Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration
The fisher reported the boat to the authorities, while critics asked why the CGA had not detected it.
The CGA said it dispatched personnel to investigate, while authorities reviewed coastal and maritime surveillance footage.
A court ordered that the two suspects be detained incommunicado and the case has been referred to the Shilin District Prosecutors’ Office.
Since last year, there have been 29 cases of illegal entry into Taiwan involving 71 people, the CGA said.
Sixty-one people in 22 cases were apprehended at the scene, giving the CGA an 85.9 percent apprehension rate, it said.
The CGA said that it has not yet sufficiently upgraded its technological equipment or integrated artificial intelligence systems to identify small targets.
Despite maximizing its workforce and radar sensitivity, it has still been unable to achieve the goal of zero unauthorized entries going undetected, it added.
A CGA task force investigation found that personnel on duty had conducted patrols along the shoreline after the boat came ashore, but overlooked some secluded areas, it said.
The personnel would be held accountable, CGA Director-General Chang Chung-lung (張忠龍) said.

Taitung issues warning on homemade alcohol sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:45 UTC
01:42:45 KST

Alcohol produced at home for personal use cannot be sold for profit, the Taitung County Finance and Economic Development Department said in a reminder to indigenous communities and tourism operators, following complaints that people were allegedly provided with homemade alcohol on paid tours.
During the summer, some indigenous communities in Taitung hold annual harvest festivals, sacred ceremonies to express gratitude and connect with ancestral spirits. Home-brewed alcohol, such as millet wine, plays a vital role in cultural exchange and rituals during the celebrations.
However, homemade alcohol may not be sold or used for commercial purposes under any circumstances, the department said, urging people to be mindful of the regulations while upholding traditions.
Photo: CNA Warning: Excessive consumption of alcohol can damage your health
Under the Tobacco and Alcohol Administration Act (菸酒管理法), people are permitted to brew a limited quantity of alcohol for personal use, up to a combined total of 100 liters of finished and semi-finished products per household annually.
Indigenous tourism has grown in popularity in the past few years, with many businesses offering paid tours that combine cultural activities, ecological tours and traditional experiences, the department said.
In some cases, operators were accused of selling homemade alcohol as part of such activities; such sales fall outside the scope of personal use and could contravene Articles 45 and 46 of the act regarding the production and sale of illegal alcohol, as paid tour programs involve commercial transactions, it said.
Tour operators who wish to provide alcoholic beverages as part of their services should use products manufactured by licensed alcohol producers to protect consumer rights and maintain a lawful business environment, the department said.
While respect for indigenous culture is important in tourism development, the county government hopes to promote indigenous traditional lifestyles as while ensuring market order and consumer safety, department Director Chang Cheng-wen (章正文) said.
Typhoon Dolphin is expected to enter the East China Sea on Saturday and intensify rainfall in western regions over the weekend as the typhoon’s outer circulation sweeps across the sea north of Taiwan, independent meteorologist Daniel Wu (吳德榮) said today. Ebola death toll in DR Congo outbreak rises to over 2,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:43 UTC
01:42:43 KST

An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) has killed 2,011 people out of 4,381 confirmed cases of the virus, officials said yesterday.
The latest toll puts it close behind the nation’s deadliest Ebola outbreak in 2018 to 2020 when nearly 2,300 people died out of 3,500 recorded cases.
The Ebola outbreak, which has hit the nation’s conflict-plagued eastern and northeastern regions, was declared on May 15, but is thought to have already been spreading for several weeks.
Photo: AFP
It is the DR Congo’s 17th surge of the highly contagious disease and is already considered the largest in the country’s history “and could well become the largest outbreak ever,” Sania Nishtar, chief executive of the Gavi global vaccine alliance, has said.
The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is estimated by Congolese health authorities to be 45.9 percent.
On Friday, WHO vaccine experts recommended a full-scale human trial of Erbovo, the only existing approved Ebola vaccine, to see if it offered cross-protection against the strain of Ebola currently spreading in the DR Congo against which no specific vaccine exists.
The Ervebo vaccine has proved safe and efficacious against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola virus and WHO experts said that early data, notably from animal trials, showed it might also give some protection against the rare Bundibugyo strain exploding in the DR Congo.
Two potential Bundibugyo vaccines are in the early stages of clinical trials on humans, while a third is being worked on to bring it to that stage.
Ebola is spread by contact with bodily fluids and causes a hemorrhagic fever.

A China Coast Guard spokesperson confirmed at the time that there had been a confrontation, but did not mention the collision, nor injuries or deaths. ====================================================================================================

Allure of 2028 Olympics draws in old guns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:42:42 UTC
01:42:42 KST

For those who have competed — or nearly competed — under the Olympic rings, the fear of missing out the next time the Games beckon is real, regardless of the venue, regardless of the sport.
Athletes who try to run it back following a lengthy sabbatical or retirement is hardly new. The list is filled with famous names, from Mark Spitz to Michael Phelps, from Lindsey Vonn to Simone Biles.
Still, the steady drip is becoming more of a torrential flow as Los Angeles 2028 approaches. The pull of the Games combined with the chance to compete at home on the world stage under the white-hot spotlight only the Olympics provide is already proving too tempting to ignore for a generation of American stars who have won medal after medal on seemingly every other continent but their own.
Photo: AP
Track icon Allyson Felix is mounting a return in her early 40s. Six-time Olympic medalist and 2020 Olympic gymnastics all-around champion Suni Lee announced last month she has started training for a shot at her third Games. Two-time Olympic gold medalist Jade Carey is back, winning the vault and finishing fifth in the all-around at the US championships over the weekend.
Asked how much of a factor the chance to compete on American soil played into her decision, Carey just smiled.
“I probably would have gone for it regardless,” said Carey, who will be 28 when the flame is lit at the Coliseum in Los Angeles, “but it does make it a little extra special that it’s in the US.”
Or maybe a lot more special. Oh, and conceivably a lot more lucrative too.
Olympic success at home can be life-changing
The media landscape has shifted dramatically since the 1996 Games in Atlanta. The rise of social media allows athletes to easily tell their stories directly to new audiences, and the ability to create and curate their own brand opens sponsorship opportunities that did not exist a generation ago.
Finding your way onto the medal stand at the Olympics anywhere in the world can make you a hero. Doing it in the US could turn you into a legend. Mary Lou Retton, Mike Eruzione and Kerri Strug know how that goes.
Longtime agent Sheryl Shade, whose list of clients over the last 30 years has included a “who’s who” of Olympians, from gymnasts Nastia Liukin and Shawn Johnson to soccer pioneer Mia Hamm and figure skater Tara Lipinski, called the opportunities for athletes to capitalize on success in Los Angeles “exponentially” greater than any Games that have come before.
“It’s going to be long-range too,” Shade said. “Because now it doesn’t end at the Olympic Games. That’s why LA is so important. This is about legacy.”
Look to “The Magnificent Seven” for proof. Three decades ago, the members of the 1996 US women’s Olympic gymnastics team walked onto the floor of the Georgia Dome for the team final as underdogs. They walked off it with gold medals around their necks, their lives forever altered.
“I mean, we all knew that was going to be special,” team captain Amanda Borden said.
Even if they had no idea how special at the time. While the group, all teenagers that summer, eventually retired and went on with their lives, to this day they get stopped by fans who remember where they were that memorable July night when the injured Strug gingerly stuck her vault landing to secure gold for the US.
They have lived the dream. In some ways, they are still living it. So no, they are not surprised that so many who have “already been there, done that” want to give it another shot.
“I can promise [for] every athlete that makes the team, this Olympics will be one of the greatest moments of their careers,” seven-time Olympic medalist Shannon Miller said.
Her advice to anyone considering it: go for it, even if things do not work out exactly as you planned.
Miller decided less than a year before the 2000 Games in Sydney to give it one final shot at age 23 — considered ancient for a gymnast at the time, although less so now. An injury at the Olympic trials ended that dream. Miller has no regrets, and a quarter century later it is considered a footnote for the most-decorated American women’s gymnast after Biles.
The attempt comes with considerable risk to mental and physical health. For every athlete that makes it, there are countless others that will not. And for those that do, the burden to succeed is ratcheted up to a level they have likely never experienced.
Dominique Moceanu, the youngest member of the Magnificent Seven, described it as a “double-edged sword.”
“You have to understand that it will be probably the biggest moment of your life,” Moceanu said. “Whether it’s because you put it on yourself or you feel the enormity of the weight of the country and the expectations. That does something to people, right?”
It does. Biles brought the discussion around mental health to the forefront of the Games in Tokyo when she removed herself from multiple nights of competition to protect herself while dealing with “the twisties.”
She took time off before returning in 2023, capping the perhaps final chapter of her career — Biles remains noncommittal about her future — by winning a second all-around gold in Paris a year later.
Skye Blakely watched Biles’ triumph from afar after her bid to make the 2024 Olympic team ended when she tore her right Achilles while training at the Olympic trials, three years after her outside shot at making the 2021 squad ended with an elbow injury at the same meet.
That has not stopped her from throwing herself into the mix once again. When describing why she continues to press on, Blakely sounds like so many American athletes across the spectrum — regardless of their resume — who feel the Games’ unique gravitational pull.
“Having a dream is always a risk if you’re going to go after it,” she said before finishing seventh in the all-around at the US championships, her first elite all-around meet in two years. “And I feel like the want for that dream has to be more than being afraid of that risk. And for me it is.”

Australia and Vietnam yesterday agreed to deepen military cooperation and support the free flow of essential trade as the two nations’ leaders met in Canberra, with both sides expressing concern over policies that threaten to disrupt global supply chains.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Vietnamese President To Lam agreed to “further strengthen defense and security engagement,” according to a joint statement released by Australia, and also vowed to do more to counter transnational organized crime and human trafficking.
In Lam’s first trip to the country as party chief and president, the two sides pledged to increase trade and investment, and support “resilient supply chains in areas such as critical minerals, semiconductors, clean energy,” they said in a separate statement.
Photo: EPA
The two nations “expressed concern” over the situation the South China Sea and reaffirmed the importance of maintaining peace, security and stability, and freedom of navigation and overflight.
They called for disputes to be resolved peacefully through legal and diplomatic processes, without the threat or use of force.
Australia and Vietnam have expanded maritime-security cooperation in the past few years, as they confront increasing Chinese aggression in the contested waters of the South China Sea. Following a visit to Danang in April, the HMAS Toowoomba trained with Vietnam People’s Navy Ship 275 off the Vietnamese coast, including search-and-rescue and ship-handling exercises.
Among the agreements reached, Vietnam would reinstate access for Australian kangaroo and deer meat, and Melbourne’s RMIT University is to expand its presence in Vietnam, with plans for a new Hanoi campus and broader operations in Ho Chi Minh City.
Two-way trade stands at more than US$14 billion, the Vietnamese government said.
Australia is also a major provider of official development assistance, supporting infrastructure and climate change resilience, it said.
Vietnam and Australia established diplomatic relations in 1973 and upgraded ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership in March 2024.
To mark the visit, Vietnamese budget carrier Vietjet Aviation JSC on Monday announced a new direct service between Ho Chi Minh City and western Sydney, scheduled to start from January next year with two round-trip services per week.
From Australia, Lam heads to New Zealand, the first visit by a Vietnamese president since 2007, where he is expected to focus on trade, investment, technology, agriculture and other areas.

Three years after his last cap for South Africa and two years after an ACL injury he thought would end his career, Deon Fourie is back in the Springboks.
Fourie, turning 40 next month, was summoned by South Africa on Monday and set to join the squad yesterday in Johannesburg to prepare for the four-match Greatest Rivalry test series against New Zealand starting on Aug. 22.
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was moved to recall Fourie after he rolled back the years for the Stormers in New Zealand’s tour opener in Cape Town on Friday.
Photo: AP
In his first match in 13 weeks, Fourie scored the Stormers’ first try, grabbed two turnovers and amazed Stormers coach John Dobson with three tackles in 15 seconds. Fourie was replaced after an hour with the score 14-14. The All Blacks prevailed 38-21.
Fourie’s value as a hybrid flanker and hooker was “invaluable,” South Africa Rugby said on Monday.
The oldest player to make his Springboks debut at 35 in 2022, Fourie played his 13th and last test in the 2023 Rugby World Cup final against New Zealand in Paris. He replaced hooker Bongi Mbonambi in the opening minutes, injured his shoulder but feared coming off and making South Africa vulnerable in the front row. They won 12-11.
Since then, he has primarily been rehabilitating.
A ruptured ACL sidelined him in 2024 from April to December. An ankle issue followed. Last season he was out from October to March with a bicep injury. In May, a croc roll tackle sent him into knee surgery.
“Over the last two years I’ve had terrible luck with injuries, and I didn’t know whether I’d be able to play this year,” Fourie said at a news conference last week before the All Blacks game.
“I’m definitely raring to go. I’ve been looking forward to this match since it was announced,” he said. “To represent your club, where I’ve spent almost my entire career, against a test side like the All Blacks is such a big occasion. To face the haka is something every little boy dreams of when they start playing rugby.”
He might get another chance in the next month.
