Hybrid Foxhound and Boxer could carry lasers, paper says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
17:32:08 BST
01:32:08 KST

Hybrid versions of Foxhound and Boxer could each carry a high-energy laser within the mass the platform is already built to take, according to a paper presented in Michigan today. The hybrid variants are modelled rather than built, though the MOD has already developed an experimental hybrid Foxhound.
A technical paper presented at the Ground Vehicle Systems Engineering and Technology Symposium in Novi, Michigan, today argues that hypothetical hybrid versions of Foxhound and Boxer could both carry a high-energy laser inside their existing payload envelopes.
The paper, by Rupert Tull de Salis of Power Size Technologies and presented by the company’s chief executive Wiktor Dotter, screens five classes of laser against both platforms using the firm’s powersize.tech simulation software and vehicle data already in the public domain.
A hybrid Foxhound could support a 60 kW laser with almost no further change to the powertrain, and 150 kW with the engine uprated from 160 kW to 228 kW. A hybrid Boxer could support 300 kW with no engine change at all, and 500 kW with an uprate from 600 kW to 704 kW. On Boxer, the paper finds the 15,000 kg mission module payload is never the limiting factor.
Both vehicles are in British Army service with conventional diesel powertrains, and the hybrid variants modelled here are hypothetical. The company states plainly that they are not proposed, funded or under development by any manufacturer or by the Ministry of Defence, and that the results are concept-stage screening outputs intended to guide early design decisions rather than detailed engineering figures.
The MOD has, however, developed an experimental hybrid Foxhound through Technology Demonstrator 6, which makes the Foxhound case less abstract than it might otherwise sound.
Why the hybrid gets the laser cheaply
The paper’s central argument is that hybridisation and laser integration are not two separate bills. Fitting a laser to a conventional diesel vehicle means bringing its entire power supply along: a dedicated generator, its own electrical distribution and the equipment to convert that power into a usable form. A hybrid has already bought most of that, because generating and moving electrical power is what its powertrain does. The paper estimates the laser’s remaining power supply requirement shrinks to little more than a converter and a filter, roughly half the weight of the standalone equivalent, and that the saving grows with the size of the laser.
The batteries are the second dividend and sized so the vehicle can observe or move without running its engine, they hold enough energy to fire the laser as well. Either vehicle could therefore engage a target with the diesel switched off, which matters because noise and exhaust heat are what give away a parked vehicle.
“Everyone in this industry knows that lasers need power and that power means hybridisation, but until now there has been no quick way to find out whether a particular vehicle can carry a particular laser before either design is frozen,” Dotter said. “If you have already hybridised a platform for silent watch and silent mobility, you have paid most of the price of putting a laser on it.”
The Foxhound squeeze
The harder problem is not the laser but the conversion as hybridising Foxhound adds around 1,100 kg of powertrain against a 2,000 kg payload, and its 7,500 kg gross vehicle mass ceiling cannot simply be raised, because heavier vehicles fall under different driving licence rules in the UK and Europe.
The paper handles this by assuming, as is normal in vehicle redesign programmes, that weight is recovered elsewhere to preserve the original payload target. That assumption is doing a considerable amount of work, and it is the point at which a sceptical reader should press. Boxer faces no equivalent pressure, with an order of magnitude more payload against a much smaller powertrain addition.
A grammar for laser weapons
Alongside the vehicle analysis, the paper proposes a classification scheme the field has so far done without. Existing discussion relies on informal shorthand such as “the 50 kW class”, which describes what a weapon draws rather than what it can defeat. The five classes set out here, A to E, run to 500 kW and are defined by target: optical sensors and small drones at the lower end, through loitering munitions and rockets, up to helicopters, fast jets and supersonic cruise missiles.
Underpinning it is a measure the paper calls the Sustained Firing Fraction. A laser cannot fire continuously, because most of the electrical power it draws becomes heat that has to be shed before the next shot. How much of an engagement a laser can actually spend firing therefore determines how much power the vehicle must supply, and the paper argues this is the least published and most important number in the entire calculation.
Timing
The analysis arrives against firm procurement signals, the 2025 Strategic Defence Review committed close to £1 billion to directed energy capability, and in June 2025 Defence Equipment and Support issued a market engagement notice for a vehicle-mounted land laser with a £20 million budget and a requirement to deploy within twelve months of contract award.
In the United States, the Army has fielded a 50 kW system on Stryker and is pursuing a 300 kW-class programme. The German Bundeswehr has ordered Skyranger 30 HEL systems on the Boxer chassis.
Dotter offered the same analysis on Stryker, a pitch as much as a finding, though the company is not without hands-on credentials in the field: Power Size personnel were previously involved in Project SWINTON, mounting and trialling a directed energy laser on a Wolfhound.
“We have built the whole analysis on open-source vehicle data so that anyone can challenge the numbers or rerun them with their own assumptions,” Dotter said. “I would far rather have that argument in a conference room than discover the problem later in a programme.”

Can the new PKK law bring peace to Turkey?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:28:00 UTC
01:28:00 KST

Can the new PKK law bring peace to Turkey?
August 11, 2026
One year ago, the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) burned its weapons in a symbolic ceremony. The move was seen as a sign of its willingness to disband. Since then, the Kurdish side has been calling on the Turkish government to take political steps.
Now, parliament has passed a bill submitted by the conservative Islamic ruling party AKP and its ultranationalist ally. Officially called the "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration," it is intended to provide the legal framework for the ongoing peace process.
According to official figures, 467 out of 592 MPs voted in favor of the bill. The ruling party and its ally see this as the beginning of a new era: Under certain conditions, the bill provides for a suspension of sentences for PKK members — but only after the PKK and its affiliated groups have been confirmed to have disbanded and disarmed, so that peace, brotherhood and solidarity can prevail throughout the entire country.
The pro-Kurdish DEM party also supports the bill, but it views it only as a first step that must be followed by further reforms.
PKK law divides society and parliament
Fierce opposition came from the ultranationalist opposition party IYI. Even during consultations, its delegate Ayyuce Turkes, daughter of the founder of the ultranationalist and right-wing extremist Grey Wolves, accused the government of rushing a landmark bill through parliament.
She also criticized what she felt was an overly conciliatory stance toward PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan. She avoided using his name, calling him a "baby killer" instead, just as government agencies and media have done for decades. There was even a physical altercation.
The debate highlights just how deep the divides are within Turkish society. While the ultranationalist IYI party rejects the process, the MHP, from which the Grey Wolves emerged, is now among its most important supporters — even though it had, previously, vehemently opposed earlier peace initiatives.
Observers believe this shift in course and the progress in the peace process are also a result of the changed security situation in the region. Among other things, they mention the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, the war in Gaza and the conflict between Israel, the United States and Iran. Syria and Iran are also home to large Kurdish populations that are supported by various regional actors.
According to the prevailing view, a more stable relationship with the Kurds who live within Turkey's own borders could provide Ankara with more leeway in domestic and foreign policy.
What's in the law?
The law applies to convictions for PKK membership, propaganda, financing or intentional support of the organization and its structures. For prison sentences of up to 15 years, enforcement is to be suspended for five years; for longer or life sentences, the suspension is to last ten years. Ongoing investigations are to be put on hold. According to pro-government media, up to 3,600 prisoners could benefit from this.
The prerequisite is the complete disbanding of the PKK and the surrender of all its weapons and ammunition. Both of these conditions have to be verified by Turkish authorities and, subsequently, officially confirmed by the National Security Council, chaired by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Excluded are PKK members who were convicted prior to June 1, 2005 — the date on which the current penal code came into force — as well as those convicted of homicide and whose convictions are final. That means the regulation does not apply to PKK founder Ocalan either. In February 2025, the 77-year-old had called on the PKK to disband, declared an end to the armed struggle and spoke out in favor of a political solution.
PKK views law as a mere first step
The PKK also calls the bill a first step; it criticizes, however, wording and content. Its key demand remained unfulfilled: As long as Ocalan cannot directly coordinate the peace process under conditions of freedom, the issue of disarmament could not be resolved either.
They said penal code regulations alone did not go far enough, more comprehensive democratization reforms were needed. The message was that as long as returning fighters or exiled politicians continued to be criminalized and were unable to engage in political activities legally, hardly any of them would leave the mountains where they've been staying.
Even legal pro-Kurdish political activity has ben restricted in Turkey for decades: parties were banned, politicians were arrested or barred from political activity. To this day, elected mayors are being removed from office, and numerous politicians and activists are in prison. Among them are two former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) that mainly represented Kurds, Selahattin Demirtas and Figen Yuksekdag.
Peace without democratization?
Political scientist Berk Esen criticizes the law for failing to offer concrete democratic solutions to the Kurdish issue. He also noted that, parallel to the peace process involving the PKK, the government had significantly increased the pressure on the largest opposition party CHP.
For about two years, the Turkish judiciary has increasingly been cracking down on leading CHP politicians. Critics view this as an attempt to weaken the government party's strongest political rival. Among the most high-profile cases is that of former mayor of Istanbul and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu. He and hundreds of other party members are in prison, on charges of fraud and corruption.
The entire CHP leadership under Ozgur Ozel was removed as well. He formed a new party several weeks ago.
Criticism of Erdogan's role
Esen primarily criticizes Erdogan's strong influence on the peace process. Although it is to be implemented by a committee chaired by the vice president and key ministers, who are also heads of the intelligence services and the National Security Council, Esen argues that it will ultimately be Erdogan as chairman of the National Security Council who decides when and which steps in the peace process will be implemented.
This assessment is also shared by Reha Ruhavioglu, director of the Kurdish Studies Center.
"Erdogan will clearly set the pace," Ruhavioglu said, attributing this to the asymmetric balance of power between the Turkish state and the PKK.
In addition, Erdogan had learned his lessons from the failure of the peace talks between 2013 and 2015 and would now certainly assemble more control in his own hands. At the same time, experts say, Erdogan has his sights set firmly on the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections, and would want to limit any political risks associated with the process.
Ruhavioglu expects further controversy, especially if former PKK fighters return to Turkey and remain at large. The government is therefore likely to allow their return, suspended sentences and political activity only gradually, and largely in response to public reaction.
This article was originally written in German.

Russia prepares its "final push" of the war this fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:27:32 UTC
01:27:32 KST

Russia prepares its 'final push' of the war this fall
Russian citizens drafted during the partial mobilization are dispatched to combat coordination areas in Moscow, Russia, on Oct. 10, 2022. (Stringer / Anadolu Agency / Getty Images)
Kostiantyn Mashovets
Military expert
In Kyiv and the capitals of its allies, talk of a brutal "winter" awaiting Ukraine because of Russian strikes is a top matter on the agenda. And it's quite likely that this very fall and winter will become Russia's own kind of "last push" — an attempt to somehow turn the tide of its war.
Back at the start of the year, I said that in 2026 the Kremlin would find it absolutely essential to achieve what it calls a "korennoy perelom v voyne" (a "fundamental turning point in the war") in order to close out the most costly and exhausting phase of the conflict on its own terms.
By early 2026, it was already obvious: Russia's continued gamble on a war "of attrition" was losing, or had already lost, any real chance of paying off.
That strategy has been dragging the Kremlin, almost irreversibly, toward its own exhaustion, and at a considerably faster clip than Ukraine has been losing its capacity to resist.
Layered on top of that are other factors: deeply negative processes are building up inside Russia itself, fueled by the war; the Kremlin's attempts to fully "cut off Ukraine's oxygen" on the international stage never quite succeeded either. Nor did Moscow get much reassurance from its "Chinese comrades," the Kremlin's chief strategic ally, who never scaled up their involvement in the war to a level that would actually cost Beijing something.
Which is to say, the Kremlin was left needing to make yet another choice about where to take its strategy next: either slide into a mode of "war on a natural fade" — in effect abandoning its core objectives, declared or otherwise, and settling for whatever it had already grabbed, which means essentially declaring an informal pause in this "age-old" standoff with Ukraine under a de facto "no peace, no war" arrangement; or move into another round of "intensified effort" and try, once more, to force Ukraine out of the war quickly, on Moscow's own terms.
Either way, the Kremlin could no longer afford to sit on that decision. Compared with where things stood at the end of 2025 and the start of 2026, the overall strategic picture kept getting worse for Moscow — and dithering had become, quite literally, a matter of survival.
So, judging by the regime's recent actions (and, in part, its rhetoric), the choice has been made — and it looks like option two.
Strategically, this is likely to unfold as follows. First comes another round of mobilization, followed by the further operational buildup of Russian forces inside Ukraine.
Next, a further ramping-up of long-range strikes across the whole of Ukraine's territory and against the main groupings of its Armed Forces — the Russians will probably try, come fall, to really "jump out of their pants," aiming to significantly degrade Ukraine's capacity to resist through nearly continuous, massed, combined long-range strikes.
Another "strategic" offensive will demand enormous resources and money, and short of "mobilizing" the economy and financial sector — including the reserves, and various forms of "dekulakization" aimed at the local oligarchy.
On top of that will come a whole package of military-economic measures inside Russia itself, most likely further state monopolization of the economy, quite possibly accelerating in both scale and pace.
Without that, the first two steps risk collapsing into a kind of caricature: another "strategic" offensive will demand enormous resources and money, and short of "mobilizing" the economy and financial sector — including the reserves, and various forms of "dekulakization" aimed at the local oligarchy — the Kremlin simply has nowhere else to pull that money from right now.
Most likely, ahead of its next "strategic lunge," the Kremlin will try to reduce market relations within its own economy to a bare minimum.
At the same time, on the socio-political front, turning Russia further into a single continuous military camp is becoming close to a prerequisite: any hint of oppositional thinking, let alone actual oppositional activity, will be punished swiftly and harshly, because you cannot run a large-scale, effective mobilization while "popular unrest" is left to smolder unchecked, let alone while dull discontent is left simmering in the background.
Which is why holding the upcoming parliamentary elections in a suitably calm and controlled manner, and further ramping up the information-psychological pressure on Russia's own population, have become non-negotiable for the Kremlin.
And finally, on the international stage, the Kremlin will obviously try with everything it has to minimize — or, where possible, block outright — any effective assistance to Ukraine, above all military-technical and financial aid, and it will try to do so in a way that ensures the volume of that aid doesn't have time to fundamentally shift Ukraine's Defense Forces' combat capability before its "final lunge" gets underway.
Still, it's worth understanding that the decisive factor in carrying out this forcibly postponed final strategic "push" will, for the Kremlin, be the military one. Because that "lunge" has to be planned, organized, prepared, and executed in practice — that is, directly on the battlefield.
The Kremlin has already grasped two basic things about its current strategic position: continuing to drag out its participation in a war this costly is dangerous, so it needs to sharply and massively "accelerate"; and while its first such attempt — I mean the ongoing Sloviansk-Kramatorsk offensive operation, which is still crawling along fairly limply — turned out, let's say, not entirely successful, it's still worth repeating with "fresh forces," "fresh people," and possibly in a "fresh location."
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Nvidia launches lightweight OpenAI model for autonomous agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:27:14 UTC
01:27:14 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
11 August 2026•Update: 11 August 2026
- Chipmaker separately announces partnerships aimed at mobilizing more than $500B for AI infrastructure
Nvidia launched Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a lightweight, customizable open artificial intelligence model on Tuesday, designed to handle high-volume tasks for autonomous agents.
The model uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 30 billion total parameters, while activating only 3 billion for each task, reducing the computing power needed to run it.
Nemotron 3.5 Lightning can be deployed on a single supported graphics processing unit GPU system, including Nvidia’s DGX Spark or H100, and has a context window of up to 1 million tokens, according to the company’s official model documentation.
The model is intended for tasks such as code review, tool use, security-alert monitoring and answering customer billing questions within larger AI-agent systems.
Nvidia said Nemotron 3.5 Lightning delivers up to four times faster output and completes agentic tasks 30% faster than other open models in its class, based on the company’s benchmark tests.
The chipmaker released the model’s weights under its OpenMDW 1.1 license, allowing businesses and developers to customize it using their own data and workflows.
Companies including cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike, legal AI provider Harvey and software-review platform CodeRabbit have tested and customized the model, said Nvidia.
Alongside the model, Nvidia introduced NeMo Switchyard, an open-source routing library that automatically directs each AI task to the most capable and cost-efficient model available.
The company said internal tests showed Switchyard preserved frontier-level accuracy while reducing task-completion costs to nearly one-third of those incurred by using Anthropic’s Opus 4.8 alone.
Nvidia seeks to mobilize over $500B for AI infrastructure
The launch came one day after Nvidia announced strategic partnerships with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to establish independent financing platforms for AI computing infrastructure.
The platforms aim to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital over time, providing dedicated pools of financing for Nvidia customers seeking to build data centers and “AI factories.”
The six financial institutions have signed memorandums of understanding, while the partnerships remain subject to final agreements.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the company had evolved from building chips to helping create a new class of productive and investable infrastructure centered on AI computing.

EU imports of Russian LNG continue to fall months ahead of an anticipated ban, but Moscow nevertheless accounted for 100% of Belgium's LNG imports in July, reveals the latest analysis by energy think tank CREA, published Aug. 10.
The report mentions that across France, Spain, and Belgium, Russian LNG imports plummeted by a combined 46%, and globally Moscow earned 36% less on LNG than it had in July.
However, "Belgium sourced all of its LNG imports in July from Russia," claims the Helsinki-based Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
The Ukrainian civil society network B4Ukraine responded to the report, saying "it is deeply shameful that ... EU countries keep sending billions of euros to Russia for fossil fuels."
According to the CREA report, Hungary and Slovakia are the top two EU countries paying for Russian fossil fuel imports, spending 486 million euros and 299 million euros in July, respectively.
The two countries remain connected to Russian pipeline networks: oil via the Druzhba pipeline, and gas via Balkan Stream.
Belgium, France, and Bulgaria rounded out the top five EU countries importing Russian fossil fuels.
The EU agreed in Jan. 2026 to a full ban on Russian LNG imports from the beginning of 2027 and on pipeline gas imports by the autumn of that year.
Globally, China remains the largest importer of Russian fossil fuels according to CREA, accounting for 43% of Russia's fossil fuel revenue.
But India, Russia's second-largest customer, recorded an all-time high for imports of Russian crude oil for the second month in a row, CREA notes.
The U.S. Senate backed a new bill that would impose tariffs on countries purchasing Russian oil and gas on Aug. 7.
If finalized, the law would impose 100% tariffs on the world's five largest buyers of Russian energy.

The website, YiyangFangchan – “fangchan” means real estate in Chinese – markets property in Yiyang, a city in Hunan province with 4 million residents where Ho Feng-shan was born in 1901.

Tibi rejection threatens Palestinian unity bid in Israel vote

Breadcrumb
Tibi rejection threatens Palestinian unity bid in Israel election
An attempt to reunite Israel's main Palestinian political parties ahead of October's election is at risk of unravelling, with the head of the committee tasked with resolving their differences telling The New Arab that the parties have a responsibility to honour the agreement they signed.
Mohammed Ali Taha, head of the Reconciliation Committee that was brought in after the parties struggled to agree among themselves, urged Ta'al leader Ahmed Tibi to reconsider his rejection of the proposed joint electoral list.
"From a moral and social perspective, in the interests of our people, in order to fight violence and this oppressive government and replace it with a less harmful one, to increase voter turnout, and for the sake of unity, everyone who signed must, as a matter of principle, honour their signature and implement the decision of the Reconciliation Committee," Taha told TNA.
The appeal came after Tibi rejected the proposed list on Sunday, throwing renewed uncertainty over an alliance that Palestinian political leaders had spent months trying to revive.
Ta'al, the Jewish-Palestinian leftist Hadash and the Palestinian nationalist Balad announced in May that they would contest the election together, reviving a political alliance that at its peak won 15 seats in the Israeli parliament.
But agreeing to reunite proved easier than deciding who would represent them.
After negotiations over the ordering of candidates reached an impasse, the three parties handed the task to the Reconciliation Committee, effectively asking an outside body to settle a dispute they had been unable to resolve themselves.
Now the committee's proposed solution has itself become the source of the latest crisis.
Taha told TNA that the committee had weighed a series of politically sensitive considerations when drawing up the list, including the relative strength of the parties and representation for Palestinian communities in the Naqab desert, where Bedouin communities face displacement and home demolitions by Israeli authorities.
Tibi was given second place on the proposed list and the chairmanship of the parliamentary bloc, Taha said, despite Balad having a larger constituency.
Two members of the Reconciliation Committee have since resigned following the breakdown in negotiations.
Ta'al declined TNA's request for comment, but has publicly described the committee's proposal as "unfair, strange, and objectionable".
'It's still not too late'
Hadash is also pressing Tibi to reverse course.
A Hadash spokesperson shared a statement with TNA from the party's new leader, Yousef Jabareen, who warned against abandoning the alliance.
"It's still not too late. We must not ignore the will of the public. We must not give up on the hope for real change: the hope for a strong, broad, and united joint list," Jabareen said. "I am optimistic. I believe we can find a formula that will be acceptable to all three lists, and together reach 10 seats."
For Jabareen, the stakes extend beyond the number of Palestinian representatives elected to the Knesset.
"This is the best way to ensure that the Netanyahu-Ben Gvir-Smotrich government does not return, and it is also the best way to build a shared future for all the citizens," he added.
Balad, which also declined TNA's request for comment, called on all three parties to meet on Monday to formally announce the joint list and approve a political programme and strategy for the election campaign.
The proposed list would place Jabareen first, followed by Tibi and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh, according to Israeli media, citing a Hadash spokesperson.
Hadash's Jafar Farah would take fourth place, followed by Balad's Bakhar Awadeh and Hadash's Ofer Cassif and Youssef Atauna.
Balad's Maha Karkabi would be eighth, followed by an unspecified Ta'al candidate and Hadash's Nihaya Washahi. Balad's Hassan Nassasra, another unspecified Ta'al candidate and Hadash's Ayas Natour would occupy the next three positions.
If the alliance secured the 10 seats Jabareen believes are within reach, Hadash would receive five, Balad three and Ta'al two, despite Tibi occupying the second position on the overall list.
That allocation is now at the centre of a dispute threatening a political reunion that its architects hoped would reverse years of fragmentation among Palestinian parties.
From 15 seats to fragmentation
The Joint List was once one of the largest blocs in the Knesset.
Hadash, Ta'al, Balad and Ra'am ran together in 2020 and won 15 seats, demonstrating the electoral strength Palestinian parties could command when united.
But the alliance subsequently fractured.
Mansour Abbas's Ra'am broke away and later joined the coalition government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid in 2021. Balad then ran separately in the 2022 election.
The renewed effort by Hadash, Ta'al and Balad to run together in October had been intended to overcome those divisions at a moment when Palestinian political representation could again prove consequential to the formation of Israel's next government.
It is also unfolding as Palestinian citizens of Israel face mounting pressure from the country's government and as far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich wield significant influence over policies affecting Palestinian communities.
For the Reconciliation Committee, the dispute now comes down to whether the parties will accept the compromise they had asked it to produce.
Taha's message to them was that the consequences of failing to do so extend beyond who occupies which place on an electoral list.

Turkey’s Kurdish region greets a conditional PKK pardon with relief, joy and doubt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:23:02 UTC
01:23:02 KST

Turkey’s Kurdish region greets a conditional PKK pardon with relief, joy and doubt
DIYARBAKIR, Turkey (AP) — Residents in Turkey’s mainly Kurdish-populated southeastern region reacted with a mix of relief, joy and uncertainty on Tuesday after parliament approved a conditional pardon for thousands of Kurdish militants, offering them a potential path toward integration into normal life in Turkey.
Lawmakers on Monday voted overwhelmingly in favor of the legislation that is aimed at advancing a peace effort between the Turkish state and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, or PKK, which waged a long-running insurgency before announcing last year that it would lay down its weapons. The measures, however, will only come into effect after Turkish authorities have verified that the group has fully disarmed.
Residents in Diyarbakir, the region’s main city, expressed hope the new law will bring peace — as well as prosperity to a region that has lagged behind economically.
“I was really very happy. I even applauded (the result) in my own home,” said 70-year-old retiree Ali Akdogan. “The economy will improve, good things will happen, people will start doing business.”
“I believe it will bring peace,” he continued, noting that since the start of the peace process there have been no deaths related to the conflict, which killed thousands of civilians, soldiers and militants over more than four decades.
Hasan Gecti, a 56-year-old shop owner, also said he believes the stability and lack of violence will benefit the region’s people economically and socially but suggested that other matters, such as greater Kurdish rights, have not been addressed.
Among other issues, Kurds have been calling for broader use of their language in education and public services, along with greater political rights, including an end to the government’s practice of ousting elected mayors and replacing them with government-appointed officials.
“Has the Kurdish issue been directly solved? That’s a bit of a question mark. In my opinion, only the terrorism problem has been solved,” Gecti said. “Unfortunately, the Kurdish issue still remains where it is.”
The PKK’s objectives evolved from independence to Kurdish rights
The PKK declared a decision to dissolve itself last year in response to a call from its imprisoned leader, Abdullah Ocalan.
The group then staged a symbolic disarmament ceremony in northern Iraq, where it is based, and announced that it was withdrawing fighters from key locations in Turkey to Iraq.
The PKK launched the insurgency in the 1980s, initially with the aim of establishing a Kurdish state in the southeast of the country. Over time, the objective evolved into a campaign for autonomy and rights for Kurds within Turkey. Kurds are estimated to make up around 15–20% of Turkey’s population.
The new legislation will suspend some prison sentences for convicted PKK members and postpone ongoing investigations and trials against others for five or 10 years, depending on the severity of the alleged offenses. If no terror-related crime is committed within the time frame, the cases will be dropped.
Turkish media reports said thousands of PKK members are likely to benefit, including those in exile in Europe and those who are based in Iraq and Syria.
Militants convicted of intentional killings and those sentenced to life terms before 2005 are excluded from the bill’s provisions. This applies to Ocalan and other senior PKK figures.
Further reforms needed, Kurdish leaders warn
Mehmet Kaya, head of the Diyarbakir Chamber of Trade and Industry, welcomed the fact that the legislation was passed with an overwhelming majority.
“It signals that violence is ending and the doors of politics are opening,” he said.
However, the law alone does not solve the Kurdish issue and that further reforms will be needed, he added.
“If the step taken from now bring sustainable democratization, social policies, and economic policies develop — which is the expectation — then the region will go through an important phase,” Kaya said.
In a statement carried by the PKK-linked ANF news outlet, the group on Monday described the Turkish legislation as a “beginning” to resolving outstanding issues but “has serious shortcomings and deficiencies.”
It called for Ocalan’s release from prison, for democratic reforms and Kurdish rights.
———
Fraser reported from Ankara, Turkey.

Taylor Swift, Lyle Lovett and more are headed for Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame

Taylor Swift, Lyle Lovett and more are headed for Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame
Global superstar Taylor Swift and country legend Lyle Lovett will be inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, the organization announced Tuesday.
The new class also includes Shawn Camp and Lee Thomas Miller, both elected in the contemporary songwriter category, and Bruce Channel as the veteran songwriter. They will be formally inducted during the 56th Anniversary Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame Gala later this year.
Swift, the 14-time Grammy Award winning artist, is elected in the contemporary songwriter/artist category. She’s known for writing many of her own hits since launching her career in Nashville as a preteen. Those include her country singles “Teardrops On My Guitar” and “Love Story,” as well as her blockbuster pop hits “Blank Space,” “Anti-Hero,” and “Cruel Summer.” She became the youngest woman ever inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in June.
Lovett is elected in the veteran songwriter/artist category. He started his career in the folk scene before finding success for his clever lyricism and innovative country-Americana songs like “She’s No Lady,” “Cowboy Man,” “Give Back My Heart,” “Why I Don’t Know,” “God Will” and more.
Camp began as a fiddle player for Shelby Lynne, Alan Jackson, Trisha Yearwood and others in the ’80s before becoming a hit songwriter. His credits include Garth Brooks’ “Two Piña Coladas,” Brooks & Dunn’s “How Long Gone” and Willie Nelson’s “A Beautiful Time.”
Miller’s hits include Terri Clark’s “I Just Wanna Be Mad,” Trace Adkins’ “You’re Gonna Miss This,” Tim McGraw’s “Nothin’ To Die For” and “Southern Girl,” Chris Stapleton’s “Whiskey And You” and many songs for Brad Paisley, including “The World.”
Texas talent Channel is perhaps best known for “Hey! Baby!” written in 1959 and recorded by José Feliciano, Ringo Starr, Conway Twitty, Anne Murray and DJ Ötzi; it may be most recognizable for its prominent placement in the 1987 film “Dirty Dancing.”
The Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame executive director Mark Ford made the announcement inside Belmont University’s R. Milton and Denice Johnson Center.
“This is always one of the most anticipated days on our calendar — the annual reveal of our incoming class,” Ford said in a statement. “We’re excited to once again add new names to a legendary list that began more than a half century ago.”

One of highest-value contracts in Israeli defense industry

Before that, the most valuable contract was the sale of Barak 8 air defense systems by Israel Aerospace Industries to India in 2017 for $1.6 billion. UK naval drones sent data to China, raising US, European fears over Chinese components -report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:16:51 UTC
01:16:51 KST

Camera components installed on UK naval drones transmitted data to an internet address in China, the Telegraph reported on Sunday.
The UK Ministry of Defense was forced to cut off all internet connectivity to the Royal Marines' £12 million fleet of K3 Scout surveillance drones after discovering that Chinese-made components were transmitting information.
The transmission was found during what the ministry said was a routine cyber-vulnerability assessment of the drones and consisted of "heartbeat communications," data that confirms the devices are online and functioning and that have the potential to share location.
However, according to a ministry spokesperson, no evidence was found that any Defense Ministry data or systems were accessed, compromised, or transmitted.
The supplier of the Royal Navy's drones, British defense contractor Kraken Technology Group, had sourced its cameras from a third party that had given it security assurances. A Kraken spokesperson said they were confident that no sensitive information had been shared and that all potential vulnerabilities had been identified and closed.
UK cuts naval drones offline after components sent data to China
The incident raised fears shared by many European countries and the US regarding Chinese-made components and machinery, the Wall Street Journal wrote on Monday.
Kraken recently won a $49 million contract from the US Special Operations Command for its drones, and the US used naval drones for the first time in combat last month, blowing up a submarine and a ship-maintenance facility in an Iranian port. The US also used a naval drone in a rescue mission off the coast of Oman in June.
According to the WSJ, drone makers rely on China specifically for brushless motors, antennas, cameras, and batteries.
Chinese components are much cheaper than those sourced elsewhere, and countries such as Ukraine, which has been going through roughly 10,000 drones a month for over a year, according to the WSJ, can't afford extra costs.
“A German electric engine is five to 10 times more expensive than a Chinese one,” Marc Wietfeld, the co-founder and chief executive of Arx Robotics, a German land-drone maker, told WSJ.
Arx Robotics has now established its supply chain in Europe, with a few components from the US to reduce its dependence on China.
"We pay the price, but we get robustness and durability in return," Wietfeld said at a recent defense show.
However, even if a defense company is willing to pay the price, it can be difficult to keep Chinese components out. While the US banned all new Chinese drones and components late last year, some tiny components in the drone sector may slip through, according to the WSJ.
“It is really, really hard to trace where the stuff comes from if you go all the way down the supply chain, and it is even harder to monitor that on an ongoing basis,” Steve Wright, a consultant who advises governments and companies on drone manufacturing, told the WSJ.
Wright added that he spends about half his time advising clients on how to keep Chinese parts out of systems.

"In my opinion, these factors are making projects more economically worthwhile than in the past. We still have a shortage of workers, but if this trend continues, the construction industry will experience a significant upgrade."
Since the war, we have heard many people in the industry talk about the inefficiency of Palestinian workers. Why did we never hear about this before?
"There was no alternative. For years, the Association of Contractors and Builders in Israel (ACBI) and other organizations of contractors tried to increase their foreign workforce, but the state refused to allow it. Despite sincere efforts and many attempts, Israeli workers did not come into the industry," Salant said.
"We were stuck with the Palestinian workers. The government did not allow us to bring high-quality foreign personnel until the war began and the entry of Palestinian workers was halted. That was the situation."
The real estate sector has undergone severe, possibly unprecedented, crises following the October 7, 2023 attack and the events that followed it. The personnel crisis was one of the worst – the entry of tens of thousands of Palestinian workers was banned overnight. There was also the problem of materials, which became both more expensive (a global trend), and less available because of Turkey's ban on exports to Israel.
"The war and the ensuing crises were certainly real problems," Hadad said.
"It was very difficult to meet the original timetable, and the state is overlooking the objective difficulties and refusing to recognize them. The state shuts down the industry for months, and no one wants to take this into account. The industry simply ground to a halt. The teams and staff, the entire activity of construction companies – things that cost a great deal of money – stopped working at the time. These things eventually caught up with us, as reflected in our profitability levels and the problems we had to overcome, but we got through it, and we're still getting through it."
Salant added that the company's prestige was what allowed it to survive the crisis.
"Our advantage is our good name. Even when there was a severe labor shortage at the beginning of the war, the workers who were available came to us. Two things are important to subcontractors: getting paid and getting paid on time. If you do that, a contractor will be loyal to you, and that's what happened. That's how we were able to narrow the gaps, and the timetable delays were confined to a few projects for a few months."
Over its four decades in the industry, Omer Construction has primarily engaged in private-sector projects. The company was recently selected to carry out the NIS 480 million Gate project at the entrance to Jerusalem and a NIS 1.2 billion residential project in Acre. The company stresses that it works solely on mega projects, not on small ones.
"If we are offered a project for NIS 50-60 million, we won't take it," Salant declares. "It's too small for us."
Like many other construction companies, Omer Construction prefers to avoid public sector tenders whenever possible. "In public tenders, whether by local authorities or the state, the decisive element in the tender is usually the price," Salant said.
"Companies seeking to win the tender make very low bids and try to make their living through changes and additions, which results in continual conflict with the party commissioning the work. That's not for us. We work in the private market with very intelligent and wise developers who know that it's better for them if their project is completed on schedule, with suitable quality, within the budget, and with the proper safety level. There are plenty of developers that wish to avoid constant friction with the contractor."
Omer Construction completed its IPO in December 2025. Today, over six months later, the company's market cap is over NIS 2 billion, and the return for the people who bought its shares is currently 68%.
Since its founding, Omer Construction has executed projects across Israel. The company currently works in three main spheres: construction, development (residential housing and urban renewal), and income-producing real estate. It also has a subsidiary, Gilmor Construction, which carries out small projects and specializes in finishing work. According to its 2025 report, the bulk of Omer Construction's revenue comes from contracting – NIS 583 million, compared with NIS 73 million from residential real estate development and NIS 8 million from income-producing real estate.
One of the company's objectives in its IPO was to reinforce and expand its activity in residential housing development, including urban renewal.
"We began working in development long before the IPO," said Omer Construction CFO Gideon Kahlon, who, together with Rosenblatt, is responsible for the company's development activity.
"In recent years, we have built a very substantial portfolio, but it is well known that development is something that takes years, especially urban renewal.
"We now have 13-14 urban renewal projects as well as development projects. When we reached the stage at which the projects required equity and investment on a fairly large scale, it became one of our considerations in holding the IPO – to raise money so that we could undertake the necessary financial investments without pressure, in the knowledge that our cash reserves could service the development projects, improve our negotiating position with the banks, and facilitate access to financial institutions."
Do you see your development business outstripping your contracting business?
"It's true that most of our current activity is in construction, but we're looking ahead to the expansion of our development activity, which will also be reflected in our reports and results and will bring us substantial rewards – not in six months, but five, six, or seven years from now," Kahalon said. "We will have a great deal of development activity coming on top of our construction activity, which will increase the volume of our business."
Was intergenerational transition a consideration?
"There is no doubt that becoming listed on the stock exchange makes an inter-generational transition easier than in a private company, but we have never been a family firm," Salant said.
"We have always believed that if a family firm does not fall apart in the second generation, it will certainly happen in the third generation. That is why my children and those of Israel Rosenblatt have never worked in the company.
"There has recently been an exception to this rule – Baruch Hadad's son, a construction engineer, is starting to work at the company – but Omer Construction is not a family firm, and there has never been any intention of making it one. It is a stable, veteran company. People work here for decades, are loyal to the company, are happy there, and look forward to going to work each day. That has always been our concept."
Where will the company be in another 10 years?
"Operations in the construction sector will continue and remain as significant as they are today. The development business will grow and provide the company with a springboard," he added.
Another important matter at the heart of the construction industry is work safety on building sites. Despite the growing attention it receives, the number of accidents remains high. 47 workers were killed on construction sites in 2025, compared with 37 in 2024 and 44 in 2023, even though the construction industry was completely shut down during part of each of these years because of the security situation.
"We emphasize safety very strongly in our company," said Salant. "One of the things we do that happens at no other company is a safety test twice a year for all the company's employees: once before Rosh Hashanah and once before Passover.
"This test is open to everyone. Those answering it correctly win cash prizes amounting to thousands of shekels. By now, this is a tradition, accompanied by a big buzz. Everyone studies the safety regulations and reviews the material in preparation for the test. This is our approach. We are very strict in this area and regard it as the most important part of everything we have spoken of – that everyone coming to the construction site in the morning should return home healthy at the end of the day.
"We work in a difficult and dangerous industry. It's not the same as sitting in a bank office. There are many risks. It's a constant battle from beginning to end. But with everything happening around us, safety is steadily improving. Once upon a time, we had to insist that workers wear safety shoes and protective helmets, but this is no longer necessary. We use technological means to keep track. We have safety supervisors and administrators. Every safety event is reported directly to the three of us — the company heads. Safety is routinely and closely monitored. We treat the small details as seriously as the big issues."
Has the entry of foreign workers had an impact in this respect?
"Yes. As soon as we switched to foreign manpower, safety improved immeasurably because they are more disciplined. With foreign workers, it's easier to keep safety under control," Salant said.

Ebola outbreak in DR Congo began months before announcement — WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:15:31 UTC
01:15:31 KST

NAIROBI, August 11. /TASS/. The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo began in February, several months before it was officially declared, Africanews reported, citing World Health Organization Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Janabi.
Genetic sequencing of the virus made it possible to establish when the outbreak began, he said. The initial cases were mistakenly diagnosed as malaria, typhoid fever or infection with a more common type of Ebola virus.
"This is a four months' delay. So we are chasing the virus. The virus is ahead of us," Janabi said at a news conference in the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia.
Many patients die because they seek medical care too late, the WHO official said. Communities outside Bunia lack medical facilities, forcing patients to travel long distances. As a result, many arrive at hospitals in critical condition.
The Ebola outbreak in DR Congo was announced on May 15. More than 4,300 cases have been confirmed so far, with over 2,000 deaths. The outbreak was caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, for which no approved vaccines or specific treatments are currently available.
Armed groups, a shortage of protective equipment and mistrust among some residents are hampering efforts to contain the disease. Ebola response workers in Kisangani told Radio Okapi that they have not received state salaries since the disease began spreading in the city, while partner organizations reimburse only their transport costs.
The current outbreak has become the fastest-spreading on record. During the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa, the deadliest by number of victims, the death toll reached 1,000 about eight months after the outbreak began.

The social partners have united around a mechanism for calculating the minimum wage from 2027. The criteria for increasing the minimum wage were agreed upon during the first round of negotiations between the government, employers and unions, held at the Ministry of Finance.
The parties agreed to implement a statutory model for increasing the minimum wage and determined the criteria by which this will be done.

Govt approves Regulations on Ministry of Communities, Territories, IDPs
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
19:14:23 EEST
01:14:23 KST

By Resolution No. 1003 of August 6, the government approved the Regulations on the Ministry of Communities, Territories, and Internally Displaced Persons of Ukraine.
According to a press release from the Ministry of Communities, from now on, a single ministry will oversee state policy in the areas of community and regional development, local self-government, support for internally displaced persons, war-affected territories, housing policy, construction, and urban planning, including accessibility policies, among others.
"A document has been adopted that defines the mandate of the new Ministry and establishes the key areas of our work. But for me, this decision has a broader significance. We cannot discuss community development, housing, support for internally displaced persons, frontline territories, reconstruction, and the future reintegration of de-occupied communities in isolation. All of these are parts of a single state policy centered on the individual and a self-reliant community," Minister for Communities, Territories, and Internally Displaced Persons Vitaliy Bezhin said in the statement.
According to the regulations, the Ministry of Communities is the lead agency within the system of central executive authorities responsible for formulating and implementing state policy in the following areas:
– state regional policy; the development of local self-government, the territorial organization of power, and the administrative-territorial structure;
– protection of critical infrastructure in the sectors for which it is responsible;
– housing policy; construction, construction standards, urban planning, spatial planning, and architecture, as well as the creation of barrier-free environments;
– technical regulation and pricing in construction (excluding public roads);
– international territorial cooperation;
– protection of the rights of forcibly displaced (deported) persons; support for territories where hostilities are (were) taking place; and matters concerning territories temporarily occupied by Russia, etc.
The Ministry of Communities also ensures the formulation and implementation of state policy in the field of architectural and construction control and supervision, the formulation of state policy in the field of ensuring energy efficiency, alternative types of liquid and solid fuels, and the implementation of state policy in the field of energy efficiency in buildings.
The full text of the Regulations on the Ministry of Communities, Territories, and Internally Displaced Persons of Ukraine is available at the following link: https://www.kmu.gov.ua/npas/deiaki-pytannia-optymizatsii-diialnosti-tsentralnykh-orhaniv-vykonavchoi-t60826.

US rights groups sue Trump over ICC sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:05:11 UTC
01:05:11 KST

Breadcrumb
US rights groups sue Trump over ICC sanctions
Rights groups on Tuesday sued US President Donald Trump over his sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court, saying the measures block victims of war crimes from pursuing justice.
The Trump administration, which rejects the ICC's authority, has imposed travel bans and asset freezes on several judges and prosecutors, primarily over their investigations into key US ally Israel.
In a New York court filing, four groups including Human Rights Watch said the sanctions should be struck down as they violate laws including First Amendment free speech protections.
"This is an unlawful abuse of power constituting a frontal attack on the rule of law, the independence of judges, prosecutors, and lawyers, basic precepts undergirding the international legal order, and the principle of equal access to justice," the lawsuit states.
The 101-page complaint says the restrictions "cause grave damage to the ability to bring to justice the perpetrators of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity."
The US sanctions, issued under an executive order Trump signed in February 2025, have targeted eight judges, three prosecutors, a UN expert and three human rights organizations.
The United Nations and the European Union previously urged Trump to reverse penalties against ICC officials.
Many of the measures were directly linked to an arrest warrant that The Hague-based court issued for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the war in Gaza.
Washington has also criticized ICC probes into alleged abuses during the US-led war in Afghanistan.
'Irreparable harm'
Tuesday's complaint, filed by HRW, American Friends Service Committee, Center for Constitutional Rights and Open Society Institute, says the sanctions have caused "profound and irreparable harm."
It states that the four groups have been forced to stop fully engaging with the ICC due to fears of civil or criminal penalties, and of being designated for sanctions themselves.
Alongside Trump, the lawsuit names Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Attorney General Todd Blanche, and Bradley Smith, director of the Office of Foreign Assets Control.
Established in 2002, the ICC prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest atrocities and acts as a last resort when countries do not have adequate legal systems to ensure accountability.
US reservations about the court predate Trump. The US, like Israel, has not ratified the international treaty that established the ICC, which is backed by nearly all Western democracies.
Russia is also not a member. Its President Vladimir Putin has been the subject of an ICC arrest warrant since March 2023.
Washington vowed last month to accelerate its campaign against the ICC beyond the existing sanctions -- accusing the court of posing "an intolerable threat to US sovereignty."
A State Department official told AFP news agency the effort would look to pressure other nations to withdraw from the court and cut off any financial support to the court.
In June, three ICC judges sanctioned by the Trump administration filed a lawsuit against the president and other senior US officials, arguing that the measures imposed on them were unlawful.
In a complaint filed in New York, Canadian judge Kimberly Prost, Uganda's Solomy Balungi Bossa and Benin's Reine Adelaide Sophie Alapini-Gansou said the sanctions were intended to "exert extrajudicial pressure."

A Russian couple near the home of Sweden's top defense executive drew a security response. The man and the woman were detained after setting up camp near the home of Saab CEO Micael Johansson, SVT Gävleborg reports.
The incident reflects the heightened security around Sweden's defense industry amid its arms supply to Ukraine. Saab makes the JAS 39 Gripen fighter, and in May, Ukraine and Sweden agreed to launch a defense deal that includes the purchase of up to 20 Gripen E/F fighters, according to Ukraine's Office of the President.
The CEO is under personal protection
Johansson lives under guard because of what Saab builds. Because of the company's military production, he is under personal protection, and he framed the security response as a routine precaution.
"My role is quite delicate. That is exactly why the guards checked these people," he said.
The property where the Russians were found does not belong to the Saab CEO himself but to a person close to him, so the couple was near, but not at, Johansson's home.
What happened at the property
The encounter began with a request to fish. A woman who spoke accented English entered the property and asked whether she could fish from the pier belonging to the plot.
She was refused, after which the guards came and took a closer look at the Russian couple.
The facts remain ambiguous
The couple's intentions are being established, and they had earlier told journalists that deportation to Russia would be risky for them because, they said, they had taken part in protests against the war in Ukraine.
That claim, if true, would run counter to a hostile-surveillance reading, though it cannot be verified either way. What the episode does show plainly is the state of alert around Sweden's defense sector amid Russia's threats.

Settlers besiege Palestinian home as Israeli army blocks aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:03:35 UTC
01:03:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Settlers besiege Palestinian family inside West Bank home as Israeli forces block help
A Palestinian family has been trapped inside its home in the occupied West Bank for three days, running short of food and unable to get medical help for a two-year-old child, as activists on the ground tell The New Arab that Israeli settlers and soldiers are preventing anyone, including an ambulance, from reaching them.
The siege of the family home in Qusra, south of Nablus, began on Sunday, when Israeli settlers erected a makeshift tent inside the grounds of the property and blocked access to the house.
Activists who have since tried to bring food and medical assistance to the family say Israeli forces have not only allowed the settlers to remain but have prevented those attempting to reach the house from getting through.
Andrey X, an activist and journalist who has spent much of the past two years documenting settler violence across the occupied West Bank, travelled to Qusra on Monday in an attempt to deliver food to the family. Instead, he said, settlers attacked his group and an ambulance in full view of Israeli soldiers.
"The settlers attacked us in full view of the army. They attacked the ambulance, and the army, instead of doing anything to the settlers, detained us and took our IDs and keys and ordered us to get out of the village, and then held us for even longer, and only then released us," Andrey told TNA.
Andrey, a Russian-born activist who holds Israeli citizenship, has spent long periods living among Palestinian communities in the West Bank, documenting settler incursions and attacks and the role of Israeli forces accompanying them.
On Monday, he said, one of the soldiers preventing access to the house appeared to endorse the settlers' claim to the land.
"One of the soldiers told me, 'It's their land. This land belongs to them,' even though this is Area B. This is a blatant violation of the Oslo Accords."
Inside the house are homeowner Yousef Hassan, his wife and their two daughters, aged two and four.
Hassan has said the family is running out of food and that his two-year-old daughter needs to see a doctor. He previously said settlers had cut electricity lines to the property.
But attempts to reach them have repeatedly failed.
Israeli forces and settlers have blocked access to the house, including for ambulances and journalists, while footage shared online showed Israeli soldiers praying alongside settlers at the makeshift encampment.
Several journalists have also been prevented from entering the area. Haaretz journalists said they were attacked by settlers while attempting to reach Qusra.
"The Israeli state is literally starving a family to death," Andrey said, describing what was happening at the house as "one of the most egregious examples of just blatant crimes against humanity being committed by the settlers and the Israeli army together".
'An attempted takeover'
Palestinian officials say the siege is part of an attempt to force the family from its property rather than an isolated confrontation.
Ameer Dawood, Director of Publishing and Documentation at the Colonisation & Wall Resistance Commission, described it to TNA as "an extremely dangerous act of settler terrorism and an attempted takeover of Palestinian property".
"The conduct of the Israeli occupation forces is particularly alarming," Dawood said, pointing to soldiers carrying out Jewish prayers alongside settlers and the prevention of an ambulance from reaching the house," he said. "This conduct provides protection and practical support for the coercive pressure being imposed on the residents."
Hassan said the pressure on his family began months before settlers established the encampment outside his home, with settlers first coming to the property and harassing them around seven months ago.
Dawood said Jabal Ras al-Ain, where the house is located, is an important agricultural area and one of Qusra's remaining spaces for natural and residential development.
"The same area has faced repeated attacks, electricity cuts and attempts to force families from their homes during recent months," he said.
The location of the confrontation is also significant.
Qusra lies in Area B of the occupied West Bank, where the Palestinian Authority exercises civil control while Israel retains overriding security powers.
Andrey had warned in an interview with TNA in June that settlers were increasingly pushing beyond Area C, which is under full Israeli control, and establishing outposts and carrying out attacks in Areas A and B.
"Setting up outposts in areas A and B was unheard of until the past few months," he said at the time. "But now they are popping up more and more."
He said those incursions could not be separated from the role of Israeli forces, describing a system in which "it's not just settlers, it's settler attacks with the support of the Israeli army who are always there".
The events outside the Hassan family's home reflect precisely the pattern activists and Palestinian officials have been warning about - settlers establishing a presence on Palestinian land while Israeli forces restrict those attempting to challenge or document it.
The siege comes amid a wider surge in Israeli settler violence and settlement expansion across the occupied West Bank, where Israeli settlements are illegal under international law.
Rights groups have documented repeated cases of settlers attacking Palestinian communities under the protection of Israeli forces, alongside land seizures, demolitions and the forced displacement of Palestinians.
Rights organisations have described the combination of settler violence and Israeli state policies as part of a broader process of state-sanctioned ethnic cleansing of the occupied West Bank.
Dawood said the Palestinian Authority, which exercises limited authority in Areas A and B, cannot physically remove the settlers and was instead seeking intervention through international organisations and diplomatic channels.
"The urgency of international intervention is heightened by the conduct of the Israeli forces at the site," he said.

Kyiv’s Kosovo conundrum: Zelenskyy’s independence comments fuel anger in Prishtina
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:03:25 UTC
01:03:25 KST

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy's first visit to Serbia was unexpected — but it was his comments on Kosovo that sparked a wave of anger in Prishtina.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s statement that Kyiv does not recognise Kosovo’s independence may have handed his Serbian counterpart Aleksandar Vučić a diplomatic win during his visit to Belgrade.
Yet it triggered a sharp backlash in Prishtina, which has demanded that Zelenskyy and Kyiv respect Kosovo's right to self-determination and the 2008 independence declaration recognised by over 100 countries, including key Western powers such as the US, the UK and 22 EU members.
During a press conference in Belgrade on Saturday, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine supports the territorial integrity of its partners and international law, in response to a question on whether Serbia could still "count on Ukraine's firm position" regarding Kosovo's independence.
Despite Prishtina's vocal support for Kyiv in Russia’s all-out war, Ukraine has not formally recognised Kosovo — Serbia's former province whose independence Belgrade does not recognise — a stance Zelenskyy said he affirmed during talks with Vučić last weekend.
"Our position ... remains unchanged. We have always stressed this, and Ukraine's policy has not changed,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s stance on Kosovo is partly based on Kyiv's insistence on protecting its own territorial integrity and continuous Russian aggression, a stance further hardened by the Russian initial invasion of Donbas in 2014 and the unilateral annexation of occupied Crimea.
Vučić has repeatedly said Serbia supports Ukraine's sovereignty over all of its lands, including Crimea, despite Belgrade refusing to align with the EU sanctions policy on Russia and maintaining a relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On Saturday, the Serbian president repeated that his country would continue to support Ukraine’s territorial integrity, including territories seized by Russia since 2014, a position Zelenskyy thanked him for.
Led by strongman Slobodan Milošević, Belgrade spent a decade cracking down on the political rights of the ethnic Albanian majority in Kosovo before tensions escalated into an armed conflict and a campaign of ethnic cleansing in 1998-1999.
A three-month NATO intervention in 1999 led to the withdrawal of Serbian troops and the UN established an executive mandate in the country for nine years, effectively maintaining a protectorate over Kosovo. It also deployed a large NATO-led peacekeeping mission, KFOR.
Kosovo then declared independence in 2008 after the recommendation of Finnish diplomat Martti Ahtisaari passed a UN General Assembly vote.
'Kosovo must be respected'
On Sunday, authorities in Kosovo responded to Zelenskyy's words by stripping down a large Ukrainian flag bearing the slogan "Free Ukraine," which had been hanging in the city's main thoroughfare since early 2022.
"The state of Kosovo must be respected," Prishtina Mayor Perparim Rama said on social media in a post showing a video of the flag being removed.
"When Kosovo is not respected, the capital Prishtina always responds in the same way," Rama added.
Rama further said that Kosovo citizens fully understand other people's struggle for freedom, dignity and the right to exist.
"Our empathy and solidarity will always be with peoples facing war, violence and persecution. Because we, better than many others, know what it means to fight for freedom, dignity and the right to exist as a state," he said.
Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca reacted by stating Prishtina "takes note with regret" of Zelenskyy's remarks, while adding that his country would continue to support Kyiv's sovereignty.
He also rejected the argument of territorial integrity as grounds for denying Kosovo's independence.
According to Konjufca, what followed after the 1999 NATO intervention "was not an act of annexation, occupation or territorial conquest, but a comprehensive international process under United Nations administration and years of internationally mediated negotiations on Kosovo’s final status."
Belgrade's balancing act
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, Belgrade has sought to balance its relationship with Moscow while furthering ties with the rest of Europe amid its ongoing EU membership bid.
Russia has long been one of Serbia's key diplomatic allies, while the Western Balkan country remains heavily dependent on Russian gas, causing Vučić to tread carefully on the matter over the past four and a half years despite repeated calls from Brussels to openly side with Ukraine.
Vučić made his first official visit to Ukraine in June 2025, attending the Ukraine–South East Europe summit in Odesa.
Unlike the other participants, he declined to sign the joint declaration even though he condemned Russia’s all-out invasion, called for the full withdrawal of Russian forces and reaffirmed support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity.
Moscow has also pointed a finger at Serbia for indirectly supplying arms to Ukraine. Russia’s foreign intelligence service SVR accused Serbia’s defence industry of “stabbing Moscow in the back” in May 2025, a claim Vučić denied.
Belgrade does not publicly supply arms to Ukraine. However, substantial quantities of Serbian-made ammunition have reportedly reached Ukraine through third countries.
The Serbian government has said it neither authorised nor controlled any such transfers.
Vučić said that he and Zelenskyy did not discuss military cooperation during the Ukrainian president's visit over the weekend.

Hong Kong urges parents not to delay childhood vaccinations as US limits jabs
All public health policies and medical recommendations must be based on scientific evidence, authorities say
The Centre for Health Protection (CHP) said on Tuesday that all public health policies and medical recommendations had to be based on scientific evidence.
“Vaccination schedules should not be altered arbitrarily without reliable scientific data or medical research supporting such changes, in order to avoid posing significant and irreversible public health risks to children,” it said.
Under the Hong Kong Childhood Immunisation Programme (HKCIP), children from birth to Primary Six are required to receive vaccines and boosters against 11 diseases – tuberculosis, poliomyelitis, hepatitis B, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, pneumococcal infection, chickenpox, measles, mumps and rubella.
Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccinations are also available for eligible primary school girls to prevent cervical cancer under the programme.
“Since delaying vaccinations reduces protection against relevant infectious diseases, the CHP reminds parents to arrange for their children to receive vaccinations in accordance with the HKCIP to ensure comprehensive and timely protection,” the centre said.
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday, recommending vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus monoclonal antibodies, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY, and dengue only for “certain high-risk groups or populations”.

====================================================================================================

Trump put a wrecking-ball through the East Wing – and through democratic norms | Francine Prose
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
16:00:03 UTC
01:00:03 KST

History has shown us how much dictators and aspiring dictators love building monuments to themselves. They enjoy reminding the world that they can do anything, no matter who is responsible for the physical labor or who will be paying the financial and human cost.
They prefer outsized structures, heroic arches, towers and columns designed to prove that their signature and their esthetic will be with us forever, even after they’re dead, though dictators often seem to believe they are too powerful to die.
There’s a chilling photograph of Hitler in the bunker beneath Berlin, not long before his suicide, contemplating an architectural model of the Austrian city of Linz which he had intended (and perhaps still intended) to rebuild to his specifications.
In Tirana, Albania, is a bizarre glass pyramid that the tyrant Enver Hoxha constructed as a museum about his life, and in which he is now buried. In Rome’s EUR, Mussolini and his city planners designed a neighborhood scaled for the race of Fascist giants to which they imagined they belonged.
So it comes as no surprise that Donald Trump has invested so much energy, sacrificed so much popular goodwill, and already spent a fortune on the East Wing ballroom, a project that will occupy an astonishing 90,000 square feet.
I can’t have been the only person who was shocked and saddened by photos of the jagged, gaping hole in the White House’s east facade, ripped apart by a wrecking crew, and by pictures of the historic rose garden remade to resemble an outdoor food court at a mall.
Also unsurprisingly, estimates of the building’s costs have varied widely, though it’s clear that the price tag will be in the hundreds of millions of dollars. ($400m is the most recent figure to have been mentioned.) Though the president has promised that the American tax payer will not be stuck with all or part of the bill, some of the money has already been diverted from publicly funded agencies such as the Secret Service.
And there’s been precious little reporting about who is getting contracts for all this expensive work and about the nature of the contractors’ relationships (financial and personal) with the president.
We were supposed to have been relieved and mollified to learn that the ballroom – a pleasure palace for the president and his most loyal and generous supporters – would occupy a mere 22,000 of those square feet. The remaining 68,000 would provide, as the president wrote in a post, “one big, expensive, and very complex unit, which is vital for National Security and Military Operations!” Beneath the ballroom, a six-story underground bunker, designed to protect our leaders in the event of an attack, will make Hitler’s roomy 3,000 square feet look, by comparison, like a studio apartment. Most recently, Trump discussed using the new building’s roof as a launching pad for killer drones and other lethal weapons.
This clever use of the air space seems to have occurred to the president even after the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia circuit ruled, in a 2-1 decision, that he could not continue renovating the East Wing without congressional approval.
According to Judges Patricia Millet and Bradley Garcia, “each president is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence”. Brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the reasoning behind the suit seems obvious: a temporary tenant cannot change a rental cottage into a skyscraper without the landlord’s permission.
The legal requirement to ask permission from Congress has already been ignored by a president who has levied tariffs, attacked Venezuela, gutted government institutions and started a war with Iran – all without bothering to consult the elected senators and representatives.
Now Trump has vowed to take the case before the US supreme court which, as we have seen, is inclined to support him, though there have been a few happy surprises when the majority of chief justices decided to uphold the constitution.
Much of what Trump does seems pointless, illogical, a response to some passing whim. But let’s not forget that he has the instincts of an autocrat, that he is the heir to a playbook, a series of actions designed to attain and consolidate increasing power and control.
This story has always been about more than a building, more than about the intentional desecration of a national symbol, of a handsome structure with a history and a meaning. We’ve seen how Trump feels about history when he accused the Smithsonian Institution of being anti-American for telling the truth about our past.
Though the case was initially brought by Alison Hoagland, an architectural historian and a board member of the National Trust, who claimed that the ballroom was an “aesthetic, cultural and historical” affront, it was never as simple as asking a town board to rule that a neighbor can’t build a view-blocking three-story vertical addition on to his house. We know, as the judges must have known, that the whole thing is about control, about the reckless grab for absolute power and about the necessity to resist it.
It might seem like a distraction – a relatively trivial concern – to worry about a building when our government agents are shooting and kidnapping innocent people on our streets. But it’s part of the same story, a narrative about the subversion – at once reckless and calculated – of our ethical and democratic norms.
Like our response to the ruined reflecting pool and the proposed Trump triumphal arch, our reaction to the proposed ballroom is partly about our wanting our grandchildren and great-grandchildren to be able to visit our nation’s capital without having to think about Donald Trump and about how much he did to deface it.
- 
  Francine Prose is a former president of PEN American Center and a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences
